Scientists on China's Tiangong space station used a laser trap to cool a clump of atoms to just above absolute zero, setting a new record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have cooled atoms to the coldest temperature ever recorded, using a laser trap aboard China's Tiangong space station.

Tiangong included an experiment in which atoms were cooled to 10 picokelvins, which is barely above absolute zero, the coldest theoretical temperature possible in physics. Absolute zero is minus 459.67 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 273.15 degrees Celsius) and the threshold at which all particles in an object are believed to stop moving.

Scientists hit the mark using "optical tweezers," known more formally as an optical-dipole trap (ODT), which hold atoms in a laser beam," the scientists reported Nov. 5 in the journal Science.

The team placed 20,000 rubidium atoms in the trap in order to restrict their motion. This reduced motion, along with the weightlessness induced by the low-gravity environment aboard the space station, caused the cloud of atoms to cool to much lower temperatures than are possible on Earth.

The experiment's results could help improve future space-based research, the team said.

"This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Despite this achievement, it's doubtful that scientists could ever hit absolute zero. One interpretation of the third law of thermodynamics, which looks at how systems behave when they approach absolute zero, is that the particles would always have a bit of entropy (disorder) associated with them, making absolute zero unachievable.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One version of the third law states that it would require an infinite number of steps to reach absolute zero, which means you will never get there," Saibal Mitra, a professor of physics at Missouri State University, told Live Science in a 2024 interview.

The second law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy always increases, would also be violated if scientists could reach absolute zero, he added. "If you had a heat sink at absolute zero, then you could build a machine that was 100% efficient," Mitra said.

That said, space makes it easier to get close to absolute zero because microgravity allows atoms to "float" and become more efficient at cooling, Science News reported. The researchers took their weightless collection of atoms and created a quantum state of matter known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which very cold atoms clump and create a "fifth state" of matter as they behave akin to a single atom.

Tiangong's very cold clump follows similar experiments on the International Space Station that reached 52 picokelvins and from a weightless fall induced by a drop from a tall tower, in which atoms hit 38 picokelvins, Science News added.

Xiong, W., Li, T., Jin, S., Huang, Q., Wang, B., Li, L., He, Y., Li, X., Chen, D., Song, T., Ji, J., Zhou, C., Lai, C., Zhang, Z., Tian, J., Guo, Y., Yao, H., Hou, X., Liu, L., . . . Chen, X. (2026). Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space. Science, eaea5324. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aea5324

#6509. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”

Over 300 Live Science readers responded to a recent poll about whether they'd train themselves to lucid dream if they could.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."

Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.

Nicoletta Lanese is the health channel editor at Live Science and was previously a news editor and staff writer at the site. She is a recipient of the 2026 AHCJ International Health Study Fellowship, with a project focused on antibiotic stewardship practices in Japan and the U.S. They hold a graduate certificate in science communication from UC Santa Cruz and degrees in neuroscience and dance from the University of Florida. Beyond Live Science, Lanese's work has appeared in The Scientist, Science News, the Mercury News, Mongabay and Stanford Medicine Magazine, among other outlets. Based in NYC, she also remains involved in dance and performs in local choreographers' work.

A new AI model, called Brain-IT, can transform brain scans into images and reverse the process, turning images into what they'd look like as brain activity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool can use brain scans to recreate the images people looked at with eerie accuracy.

The system, called Brain-IT, uses data from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure activity in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes visual input. A computer model then predicts both the broad layout of an image and high-level information about its content. It then passes those predictions to an AI image generator, researchers explained in a study uploaded to the preprint database arXiv. The research was presented at the ICLR 2026 conference, held April 23-25, and publicized by its authors in September.

Brain-IT builds on an approach called the Universal Brain Encoder. That model begins with an image and then predicts the fMRI response that would be expected in individual "voxels" ‪—‬ small 3D units ‪—‬ in a brain scan.

"The key idea is that every voxel, a tiny cube of brain tissue, gets its own learned vector that captures what it cares about in images," said study first author Roman Beliy, a doctoral candidate in the Department of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel.

Some voxels may be tuned to relatively simple elements of an image, such as edges, textures or locations. Others might be responding to higher-level abstract categories, like faces, bodies or scenes.

Traditional image-to-fMRI systems have generally been custom trained for each participant and dataset. The Universal Brain Encoder is more flexible. It learns from data from multiple people and can transfer information across participants, datasets or different MRI systems with varying magnetic-field strengths, according to the study.

A voxel can determine which parts of an image are relevant to it based on its learned profile, essentially saying, "I recognize edges. Which parts of this image are edges?"

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The Universal Brain Encoder starts with an image and predicts brain activity; Brain-IT starts with measured brain activity and reconstructs the image the person saw. In other words,it asks "based on this brain activity, what was the subject looking at?". It sorts thousands of tiny brain-scan measurements from the visual cortex into 128 groups based on the kinds of visual information they tend to carry.

The system then lets those groups share clues with one another, allowing it to combine, for example, information about a scene's shape, color and possible objects, to build a more complete picture of the image, Beliy explained.

The decoder produces two types of visual predictions. One captures semantic information ‪—‬ the features associated with what is likely in a scene; for an image of a dog standing in grass, for instance, this would include things like the features of a dog and an outdoor, grassy setting. The other captures structural information, like the broad visual layout or how forms are arranged.

In the above example, this would be aspects like the outline of the dog or where it was positioned in the frame. The structural prediction gives the generator a starting point for the image, rather than beginning from pure noise, while the semantic info guides an image generator that removes the remaining static until the image emerges.

Although the new tool can recreate what people see, it can't reproduce memories or imagined scenes.

"We're not reading people's thoughts," study co-author Michal Irani, a computer scientist at the Weizmann Institute of Science, told Live Science. "The images we do manage to recover from fMRI require people's cooperation and full intended collaboration."

The original image of a baseball game (left) and the reconstruction (right) generated by the Brain-IT AI model based on the brain activity of a person viewing the image.

Brain-IT's synthetic images were compared with the images that participants saw. Brain-IT surpassed prior leading methods on standard objective reconstruction metrics and produced more faithful results, the study authors wrote. The system shined when limited fMRI data from a new participant was available, with just one hour of data from a new participant producing results as accurately as earlier approaches that had been trained on 40 hours of recordings.

A high-scoring or realistic-looking output should not be mistaken for a perfect copy of what someone saw, however.

In the final stage of processing, the system uses an off-the-shelf diffusion generator trained on massive numbers of images. Models like this generate plausible images and can smooth textures, sharpen facial features or fill in missing details.

Beliy said this "beautification" can make reconstructions more polished and convincing and introduce details that don't necessarily come from the brain data itself. In other words, the scan constrains the generated picture, but the AI model supplies some of its realism from learned patterns in photographs.

While the new system produces impressive results for seen images, it can't be used to reconstruct an imagined or remembered image.

"Brain-IT relies on how the brain processes a seen image," Irani said. "Information flows from the eyes to the primary visual cortex and onward through a series of visual areas that recognize objects and scenes."

In a controlled experiment, researchers also know precisely which image was shown, giving the model a target during training and evaluation. In contrast, memories and imagined images do not offer the same clean reference. They can be vague and shaped by brain networks involved in memory and thought, with only partial and weaker reactivation of visual regions, Irani said. One limitation that would prevent this technology from being widely deployed is that the only way to get reliable results is from fMRI scanning, which is cumbersome and expensive. The team is currently experimenting with using easier-to-collect electroencephalogram (EEG) data, which is obtained via electrodes on the head, but that work is in the very preliminary stages, according to Irani.

The new system could help brain researchers better understand which visual information is represented in different brain regions, how those regions interact and how individuals’ patterns differ. Such tools could eventually reveal differences in visual processing that could help clinicians spot neurological, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.

"There are numerous useful medical applications which we are currently striving toward," Irani said. "These include using our brain encoder/decoder to detect and analyze brain disorders such as MS, PTSD, autism and psychiatric disorders."

Beliy, R., Zalcher, A., Kogman, J., Wasserman, N., & Irani, M. (2025, October 29). Brain-IT: Image Reconstruction from fMRI via Brain-Interaction Transformer. arXiv.org. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25976

A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have company this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is currently orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.

#6496. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.

#6493. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6488. Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

L. Davin et al. Modeling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia. PLOS One. 2026. doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360388

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.

The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) officially announced its decision to revoke the United States' measles elimination status on Nov. 17, 2026. The week prior, the Wall Street Journal reported that the PAHO had reached that decision.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

The U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

"When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

It takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

The nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in New York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.

#6484. The 8 Best MagSafe-Compatible Portable Chargers For On-the-Go Charging

A magnetic battery pack snaps onto your phone and keeps it going all day, no cable needed.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A good portable battery pack keeps your phone alive through long travel days, packed schedules, and everything in between. If you have a MagSafe iPhone (the iPhone 12 or newer) or an Android phone that supports Qi2, a magnetic pack is the most convenient choice: it clicks onto the back of our favorite phones and starts charging, with no cable to carry.

These packs have come a long way. The first MagSafe batteries charged at a sluggish 5 watts. Many of today’s Qi2 packs deliver 15 watts, and the newest Qi2.2 models reach 25 watts while fitting twice the battery into a body about as thin as your phone. Plenty also add built-in cables, kickstands, and fast USB-C ports for topping up a second device.

All that progress means more choice, and more spec sheets that look the same. We’ve rounded up the best MagSafe portable chargers you can buy right now, from slim everyday packs to fast premium picks, so you can find the right one for you.

I’ve used MagSafe battery packs with my iPhone for years. The ones I kept using had a strong magnet and enough battery to get through a day away from an outlet. Most picks here support Qi2, which charges at 15 watts, or Qi2.2, which charges at up to 25 watts on an iPhone 16 or newer. I looked for packs around 10,000 mAh, since that size can charge most phones and then some. I also looked for a USB-C port of 30 watts or more, so the pack itself recharges quickly.

The INIU SnapGo Air packs a 10,000 mAh battery into a body just half an inch thick. It supports Qi2.2 wireless charging at up to 25 watts, and INIU says it can take an iPhone 17 Pro from empty to 50 percent in 33 minutes. That top speed works on the iPhone 16 Plus, 16 Pro Max, and newer models running iOS 26. The iPhone 12 through 15 charge at 15 watts.

For faster charging, plug in the USB-C cable attached to the pack. It delivers 45 watts, which INIU says charges an iPhone 17 Pro from 20 to 78 percent in 25 minutes. The pack also supports passthrough charging, so when it’s plugged into the wall, it charges itself and your phone at the same time. The cable doubles as a lanyard and detaches, and a digital display shows the exact battery percentage.

For $23, the LISEN Ultra Slim charges at the same 15-watt Qi2 speed as the Anker Nano, which costs more than twice as much. It’s 0.38 inches thick and weighs 3.6 ounces. LISEN says it charges an iPhone 17 to about 50 percent in an hour. Past 75 percent, it slows down on purpose to protect your phone’s battery.

LISEN lists the battery as 5,000 mAh but gives a rated capacity of 3,000 mAh. The rated number is closer to how much charge reaches your phone, so plan on a partial top-up rather than a full charge. Plugged in with a USB-C cable, it charges at up to 20 watts. It only works with the iPhone 12 through 18. LISEN recommends pairing it with a MagSafe case, since other cases can cause overheating.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro costs twice as much as our top pick, and most of that extra money goes toward cooling. Wireless charging creates heat, and many packs slow down as they warm up. This one has a small fan and layers of graphene that Anker says keep it cool, so it can stay at its top speed of 25 watts for longer. It’s rated to charge an iPhone 18 Pro to 50 percent in 25 minutes.

Its USB-C port runs at 45 watts in both directions, fast enough to refill the pack from 0 to 80 percent in under an hour. A screen shows battery level, charging speed, temperature, and battery health, and a built-in stand folds out to prop up your phone for video.

UGREEN says the MagFlow can fully charge an iPhone 17 Pro Max more than 2.5 times before it needs a wall outlet. At 20,000 mAh, it holds twice as much as our top pick, and a digital display on the side shows how much is left.

Wireless charging runs at up to 25 watts, which UGREEN says gets an iPhone 18 Pro to 50 percent in 30 minutes. The built-in USB-C cable on the side doubles as a carry strap, and UGREEN rates it for more than 10,000 bends. The pack's USB-C port charges at up to 45 watts and refills the pack at the same rate, and a USB-A port lets you plug in older cables.

Fitting twice the battery makes the MagFlow heavier and thicker than our 10,000 mAh picks. That makes it harder to slip into a pocket, and it adds noticeable weight to the back of your phone while it charges.

The Sharge Icemag 3 has a see-through case that shows the internal components, plus a subtle RGB light. It charges wirelessly at up to 25 watts using Qi2.2, and Sharge says that gets an iPhone 17 Pro from zero to 50 percent in 30 minutes. A built-in fan keeps the pack’s surface cool, so charging stays steady. The fan doesn't lower your phone's temperature.

A fold-out kickstand holds your phone upright or sideways for video calls. The built-in USB-C cable and a second USB-C port sit on the side, so you can still hold your phone normally while it charges via cable. Unlike the previous two picks, the wired connection charges a bit slower at up to 35 watts.

The Anker Nano Magnetic Power Bank is 0.34 inches thick and weighs 4.3 ounces, about a third less than the INIU. Because it’s Qi2 rather than Qi2.2, it charges wirelessly at up to 15 watts. Its 5,000 mAh battery is half the size of our other picks, but that makes it more pocketable.

Anker’s own figures show it charging an iPhone 17 to 85 percent and an iPhone 17 Pro Max to 63 percent with the phone in Low Power Mode. That makes it a backup for a long day, not a full refill. A graphene layer inside spreads heat, so the pack stays cool. The USB-C port charges a phone at up to 20 watts, and the pack comes in six colors with a two-year warranty.

If you take your phone on hikes or to the beach, the TORRAS MiniMag Pro is the magnetic pack to get. TORRAS rates it IP54, so it should be protected from dust and splashes from any direction; however, it isn't meant for underwater use.

Inside is a semi-solid-state battery that TORRAS says passed puncture, crush, and drop testing. An aluminum frame wraps the body, and a digital display shows the remaining charge.

Wireless charging tops out at 15 watts, and with a USB-C cable, the pack charges a phone at up to 30 watts. With passthrough charging, one cable plugged into the wall charges the pack and your phone together overnight.

The iPhone Air gave up battery capacity to get its thin body, and Apple’s answer is a battery pack built just for it. On the Air, Apple says it adds up to 65 percent more charge. The pack is shaped around the Air's camera bump, so it doesn't fit other iPhones.

While it fits the Air perfectly, wireless charging tops out at 12 watts. For faster top-ups, leave the battery attached and plug your phone into a 25-watt or higher adapter; the phone and battery charge together. The pack also has no battery readout. Instead, a single hidden light glows green while it charges and orange when it runs low.

Check the box for Qi2 or Qi2.2. Qi2 packs charge wirelessly at up to 15 watts, while Qi2.2 packs reach 25 watts, which Apple says can bring an iPhone 17 Pro to 50 percent in about 30 minutes. Packs sold as "magnetic" or "MagSafe-compatible" without Qi2 certification often charge at just 7.5 watts.

The iPhone 12 through 15 charge at 15 watts even on a Qi2.2 pack, so if you own one, a cheaper Qi2 pack will charge it just as fast. For 25 watts, you need a newer phone, such as the iPhone 16 series and later models running iOS 26.

For most people, I recommend a pack around 10,000 mAh, the size of our top pick. Don't expect two full charges, though. Some power is lost in the battery cells and in the circuits that convert it for your phone. Anker says its 10,000 mAh pack delivers about 5,500 to 6,500 mAh to your phone. A 5,000 mAh pack is thinner and lighter, but it works best as a midday top-up. A 20,000 mAh pack can recharge a phone several times, but the extra weight and thickness make it harder to carry.

Every magnetic pack has a USB-C port, which refills the pack and can charge a second device. Look for one rated at 30 watts or higher. At 45 watts, a pack can fast-charge a phone over a cable and refill itself quickly. Anker says the MagGo 2 Pro reaches 80 percent in 52 minutes. If you want to charge the pack and your phone overnight from one outlet, look for passthrough charging.

Faster wireless charging produces more heat, and many packs cut their charging speed as they warm up. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro and Sharge Icemag 3 use small fans to maintain speed. Thick cases trap heat too. Anker recommends a case no thicker than 2.4 mm.

Most magnetic packs are designed around iPhones. Anker and LISEN don't recommend their packs for Android phones, and Apple’s own battery fits only the iPhone Air. If you use a case, make sure it's MagSafe-compatible, or the magnet won't hold well.

#6483. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night."

Trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over."

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly."

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of our DNA," geneticist Turi King examines how DNA was used to reveal the ultimate fate of the last members of the House of Romanov.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In 1917, the Russian Revolution was in full swing. Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated, and he and his family were exiled to a remote Siberian town. There were plans to get the family to the U.K., but King George V (Nicholas' first cousin) and the British government withdrew their offer of asylum over concerns of the ramifications.

After the Russian Provisional Government was overthrown by the more extreme Bolsheviks in October 1917, Nicholas, his wife, their children and several members of the family's staff were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, where, in July 1918, they were executed. Their bodies were hidden and remained lost to time ‪for nearly a century —‬ until modern technology, with some help from the British royal family, unraveled the fascinating story of their disappearance.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of Our DNA: How Genetics Has Changed the World" (Pegasus Books, 2026), author Turi King, director of the Center for Evolution at the University of Bath, looks back at the incredible story of how DNA was used to solve a major mystery of modern history: What happened to the last members of the House of Romanov?

I was sitting in a lecture theatre at Cambridge University in 1994 when one of my lecturers, Erika Hagelberg, spoke about a new study she had just been involved in. It was the first major case to combine both mitochondrial DNA and DNA fingerprinting to identify human remains: those of the Russian imperial family.

But first I need to take you back to Russia in 1917 and the abdication of the tsar following the Russian Revolution.

The Russian royal family, the Romanovs, had been the reigning imperial dynasty since 1617, and three centuries later, Tsar Nicholas II was on the throne. Nicholas was the cousin of George V, king of the United Kingdom, their mothers being sisters, and had married George's cousin Princess Alix (Alexandra) of Hesse, who was apparently Queen Victoria's favourite grandchild. Nicholas and Alix had five children, four daughters (Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia) and a son, Alexei.

The tsar and his wife were not well liked by the Russian population and political unrest culminated in the revolution of 1917, when Nicholas was forced to abdicate. The family were kept under house arrest and in 1918 they were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg with the royal physician, Dr Botkin, and three of their staff. On the night of 16 July, the family, their doctor and staff were herded into the cellar together and executed. Their bodies were then taken to a secret location and placed in a hastily dug communal grave, doused in sulphuric acid in an attempt to disfigure them and hinder identification, and then covered over, the location of the grave being lost for more than 70 years.

The Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, 1919.

Ironically, the new Russian government had wanted to get the Romanovs out of Russia due to the risk of their becoming a rallying point, but a plan to grant asylum to the Romanovs in the U.K. because of their links with the British royal family fell through, owing to a reluctance on the part of George V to grant it. Yet those links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial in their identification.

Fast-forward to 1991, when several skeletons were found in a shallow grave some 20 miles from Yekaterinburg. Many of the bones were badly damaged but it was possible to determine, based on examination of the skeletal remains, that there were nine individuals — two short of the 11 killed that night. The faces of the skulls were badly damaged in all of the skeletons, all of them showing evidence of violence either in the form of bullet holes or bayonet wounds or both. Before the genetic study, Russian forensic scientists had used numerous techniques alongside historical data to tentatively identify the remains as some of the members of the Russian royal family, their doctor and servants.

These included examining the bones, to determine approximate age and sex, and some of the teeth, the expensive dental work, incorporating gold, platinum and porcelain, indicating that certain remains must belong to members of an aristocratic family. The team worked out that the two missing individuals would have been two of the children, one of the daughters (while it was hard to determine which one it would be, given how close in age they were, it was thought that it was either Maria or Anastasia) and the son, Prince Alexei.

The Russian chief forensic medical examiner then contacted a team in the U.K., which included Erika, to see if genetic evidence could be used to confirm the identification. The U.K. team used the amelogenin genetic sex test, now part of standard forensic DNA testing, which confirmed the sex of the skeletons (four male and five female bodies), while an early form of DNA profiling showed that there was a family group here — two parents and three children — and four unrelated individuals. So far, so good.

Next, they needed to prove that this was the Russian royal family, and they did this using mitochondrial DNA analysis. As you'll remember, mitochondrial DNA is passed down by a mother to all her children, male and female, but only daughters can pass it on — so if female-line family members of Tsar Nicholas and Tsarina Alexandra could be found and would agree to give a DNA test, their mitochondrial DNA should match that of their royal ancestors. It just so happened that the late Prince Philip, husband of the late Queen Elizabeth, was related to the tsarina through the female line: she was his great-aunt, his maternal grandmother being the sister of the tsarina. He kindly gave a DNA sample.

The testing that they did was standard for the time in that they looked at two regions known as hypervariable regions 1 and 2 (HVR1 and HVR2). You'll remember that mitochondrial DNA has 37 rather crucial genes on it where any "typo" that occurs as the DNA is being copied could have serious consequences if the mutation is deleterious. By contrast, in those parts of the mitochondrial genome that don't code for anything, such as these two hypervariable regions, mutations can occur more freely without necessarily causing issues, meaning that these regions contain much more genetic variation. These are the sections of mitochondrial DNA that scientists began analysing for identification purposes. While it's not as precise as DNA profiling because many thousands of people will all have the same mitochondrial DNA type, it can be very helpful in a case such as this.

Prince Philip's DNA was eventually used to confirm the identities of the lost Romanov family.

When the team sequenced these two regions, Prince Philip's mitochondrial DNA was found to match that of the putative remains of the tsarina and her daughters. Next they found two living female-line relatives of the tsar, descended from his maternal grandmother: a great-great-niece, Princess Xenia Cheremeteff Sfiris, and a first cousin twice removed, James Carnegie, 3rd Duke of Fife. The mitochondrial DNA from these two matched each other perfectly, and they, in turn, matched that of the tsar, except at one base where there was both a match and a mismatch.

This is because the tsar had what's known as a heteroplasmy at this position: some of the mitochondrial DNA sequences showed a T and others showed a C, his maternal relatives showing a T. Heteroplasmy is known to take place primarily through mutations occurring when the DNA is copied to make new cells in a person's lifetime, but it can be inherited from a maternal ancestor with heteroplasmy. Extremely rarely, it can come from paternal mitochondrial DNA making it into the cell. So the fact that heteroplasmy existed in the DNA sample didn't negate the match, and the probability that these were the Romanovs was still between 70 to 1 through to 840,000 to 1 in favour. But, it did sow some seeds of doubt. Incidentally, we now know that heteroplasmy is fairly common, with potentially over half of the human population having at least one heteroplasmy, albeit at a low percentage in terms of their mitochondrial DNA carrying it.

So, to be doubly sure, in 1996 the remains of the tsar's brother, Georgij, who had died in 1899, were exhumed and he was found to have exactly the same mitochondrial heteroplasmy. Given the very low chance of two people having this particular heteroplasmy if they weren't related, this pointed to the mitochondrial DNA data the researchers obtained being 130,000,000 times more likely if these were the Romanovs than if they were an unrelated family.

The case was solved in terms of identifying the tsar, tsarina and three of their daughters, but the mystery still remained as to what had happened to the two other children. In the scientific paper reporting the results, the authors conjectured that possibly the two children had been buried separately, or that they could have survived the massacre. Incidentally, there was a woman living in the U.S. who claimed to be Anastasia, saying she had managed to escape being executed, and so the fact that two of the children were missing from the Romanov family group only fuelled the idea that maybe she truly was the missing princess.

Then, in 2007, a group of amateur archaeologists, digging a mere 70 metres away from the previously discovered mass grave, came across more human remains. Skeletal evidence showed that they were the remains of two bodies, a young woman aged 15-19 and a probable male aged 12-15. DNA analysis was brought to bear and again showed that the two individuals were siblings and related to the Romanovs already identified. As an extra DNA test, Y-chromosome testing was carried out, the Y chromosome being passed from father to son, to confirm that the Y chromosome of the newly found male skeleton was indeed male and that it matched the Y chromosome of the tsar. This also then matched male-line relatives — a second cousin once removed of the tsar (third cousin of Alexei) through Tsar Nicholas I. The missing Romanov children had been found.
