#6480. Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Asteroid defense is the mission’s top priority, but there’s also fascinating science to be done.

The Hera spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera captured this black-and-white image of Didymos and Dimorphos from about 60 kilometers away. The photo shows the far side of Didymos compared to the DART impact.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

Think that cows are the king of flatulence? There's another animal that likely blows the competition away.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Flatology, the study of flatulence, sounds more like a joke than a serious scientific discipline. But studying farts actually helps biologists understand an animal's diet and digestion.

We know that a host of creatures ‪—​​ from whales, to snakes, to sloths ‪— pass gas. But do we know which animal is the top tooter? Experts told Live Science the answer is blowing in the wind.

"Getting quantitative measurements for farts per animal is pretty difficult," Nick Caruso, a data scientist and co-author of '"Does It Fart?: The Definitive Field Guide to Animal Flatulence'' (Quercus Publishing, 2017), told Live Science in an email.

What we can do is hypothesize using the data we do have. Expelled gas is made partially of methane, so comparing methane emissions produced by different species may provide a clue. However, this method does have limitations, experts pointed out.

Researchers measure the methane animals produce by placing them inside respiration chambers, then inserting a capsule into the stomach that releases a tracer gas while strapping them with a harness that samples their breath. Alternatively, they capture their breath at stations where they feed or are milked.

Research points to livestock, especially cows, as major methane emitters. A recent report puts their total methane emissions at 117 teragrams per year. (One teragram is equal to 1 billion kilograms, or 2.2 billion pounds.) A buildup of cow-generated methane gas even caused a dairy shed in Germany to explode. However, contrary to what many people believe, the "overwhelming majority" of methane emissions from livestock is released through burping, not flatulence, Ermias Kebreab, a professor of animal science at the University of California, Davis, told Live Science in an email.

The reason comes down to where in the gut the gas is made. Herbivores can't break down plant material on their own; they rely on microbes in their guts to ferment it, and that fermentation releases gases such as methane and carbon dioxide, Dr. Marcus Clauss, head of research and co-director of the Clinic for Zoo Animals, Exotic Pets and Wildlife at the University of Zurich, told Live Science in an email. Some of this gas is absorbed into the bloodstream and exhaled. The rest tends to leave by the nearest exit ‪—‬ animals that ferment their food toward the front of the digestive tract mostly burp it out, while those that ferment it toward the back mostly pass it as wind, Clauss explained.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Cows and other ruminants ‪(such as buffalo, sheep, goats and camels)‬ ferment their food in a chamber called the rumen, located near the front of the digestive system, so most of the methane they produce is through belching, Matthew Hayek, an associate professor of environmental studies at New York University, told Live Science in an email.

So if it's not cows, which animal is the top farter based on their methane emissions? The best candidates are hindgut fermenters ‪—‬ herbivores that digest plant matter in the large intestine (the hindgut). Meat eaters, by contrast, typically produce far less methane than herbivores do, Clauss said.

Are cows really the top contender for animal farts?

One possible contender are termites, which break down wood and grass in their hindguts. Their global population is estimated to be around 27 quadrillion (that's 15 zeros) individuals, and they collectively emit 10 teragrams of methane per year.

But, per individual, the title might go to horses. According to a 2019 report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, horses have the highest methane emissions among hindgut fermenters — around 40 pounds (18 kg) of methane per horse each year.

However, Clauss is skeptical. "The ranking of horse as highest is only because it has been measured," he told Live Science in an email. "But there are so many hindgut fermenters not measured, like rhino ... Who knows?"

If we consider methane emissions per unit of bodyweight, the nutria (Myocastor coypus) ‪—‬ an herbivorous, semiaquatic rodent ‪—‬ would have higher methane emissions than the horse, Clauss said.

Clauss also questioned the accuracy of using methane emissions data as an indicator of flatulence. "There is some methane in flatulence, but most likely the majority of methane produced by an animal is exhaled, i.e. it goes via blood to the lungs," he said.

So until scientists figure out how to measure animal farts, any ranking remains speculative. For now, scientists have developed ways to track intestinal gas in people, including swallowable electronic capsules that measure gases inside the gut and clip-on underwear sensors that detect hydrogen in farts.

Methane is a particularly potent greenhouse gas when released into the atmosphere, and the quantities that large herds of cows and other ruminants emit through burping are enough to contribute to climate change. Indeed, scientists are experimenting with ways to reduce methane emissions from cattle — for example, by adding seaweed to their diet.

But animal flatulence is not a major contributor to global methane increases, Hayek said.

Even methane emissions from termite flatulence, while large, do not have an impact, Stefan Arndt, a professor of physiological and ecosystem ecology at the University of Melbourne in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "A large proportion of that methane is then consumed by methanotrophic bacteria in the soil," he said. These bacteria use methane as an energy source, thereby reducing the net methane emissions from termites substantially.

"Their emissions are part of the natural cycle of methane that has always been there for millennia," Arndt added. "The increasing methane concentrations in the atmosphere that are leading to climate change are caused by humans."

#6477. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially launched his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

#6476. The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A new study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

After nine days in space, the Artemis II crewmembers faced their final and riskiest challenge: splashdown. In this excerpt from the book "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space," astronaut Jeremy Hansen describes the moment from his chair.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After nine days in space, the four crewmembers of NASA's Artemis II mission looked out their capsule window on April 10, 2026, and saw the bright-blue Earth below them. The crew had traveled more than 250,000 miles (400,000 kilometers) from our planet — farther from Earth than any humans had ever gone — and now, home was just a few hundred miles straight down.

Only one milestone remained: splashdown, a fast and fiery plunge into the Pacific Ocean that would mark the end of humanity's first crewed mission to the moon in more than 50 years.Mission specialist Jeremy Hansen, the lone Canadian Space Agency astronaut on the crew, had every reason to be confident that the team's Orion crew capsule would hold up just fine. But this was Hansen's first time in space, and his first time dropping through the sky like a fireball at 24,600 mph (39,600 kmh).

It wasn't that he was afraid for himself, Hansen explains in "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space" (Hanover Square Press, 2026), which he co-wrote with John Larsen). Rather, he knew that his wife Catherine and three children would be among the millions of Earthlings watching the most dangerous moment of his mission from below.

In this excerpt from the book, Hansen describes the thrilling intensity of splashdown and the euphoria of knowing that he and his crewmates were going to make it back safely — and make history.

CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen smiles inside the Orion crew capsule during the Artemis II lunar flyby.

Immediately after jettisoning the European Service Module, and exactly half an hour before we were due to splashdown, Mission Control initiated the crew module raise burn. This nineteen-second burn was the first and only burn using the small thrusters built into our Orion capsule. It slightly shallowed our entry trajectory to put us right in the sweet spot while also providing some added distance from the service module, as we'd be hitting the atmosphere in near succession. It, too, went flawlessly. I tightened my straps; it was time for the fireworks.

A re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere is absolutely on the short list of the most incredible experiences of my life. We slammed into it at 7:53 p.m., thundering down at over 10 kilometres [6.2 miles] per second. Per second.

The thrusters fired almost constantly to stabilize the capsule: loud thuds, as if Thor himself were hammering on our spacecraft, as the G-forces quickly began to build, aggressively scrubbing off the velocity we had added to our rocket nine days earlier. Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us. It started red and transformed into a bright, bluish-green, pulsating light. It was breathtaking, the bright colors igniting our senses.

It was insane to think about what we were doing. We all knew how this worked; we all knew the science. But deep inside, I also recognized that astronauts must have a screw loose to do this. Nobody in their right mind would strap themselves inside a metal canister that itself was sitting inside a giant fireball. But there was no other way down, and I had accepted the realities of this journey long in advance.

Although I was at peace, I felt guilty for the stress I was putting on my family. I had talked to them openly about the mission's risks, and this was the highest-risk moment. I tried to send my love telepathically, telling them it was going great.

The Orion capsule drops toward the Pacific Ocean with all parachutes successfully deployed.

As we continued our freefall, it looked like a thousand camera flashes were exploding inside Integrity. I lowered the sun visor on my helmet. There were only centimeters of heatshield and aluminum separating me from the more than 2500°C heat outside. Almost instantly, the heat inside our cramped home also began to rise, an increase that engineers refer to as "thermally benign." All I know is that I couldn't feel it, blissfully wrapped in my thermally controlled garments.

As we continued to fall, the G-forces built up to nearly four times the pressure we feel on Earth. I wasn't too worried, having endured more than five minutes of the same G-force, or more, in the NASA centrifuge trainer. I had half-expected the freefall back to Earth to seem short, but it was a long six minutes before the flames finally ceased and we re-established communications with Mission Control.

It had already been a wild ride, but I also knew another crazy part — parachute deployment and the actual splashdown — lay ahead. My adrenalin kept pumping.

Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us.

"Integrity, Houston. Comms check, post-blackout," we heard from Mission Control. It was music to our ears. It was exactly 8:00 p.m.

"Houston, Integrity," Reid [Wiseman, mission commander], replied. "We have you loud and clear."

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried. For the folks at NASA, it was clear that all had gone well during the descent — a small fleet of NASA and Air Force planes had captured it on high-resolution cameras. But, for me, it wasn't over yet. I wouldn't truly feel safe until our three main parachutes successfully deployed. If they didn't, we'd be a chunk of metal slamming into the ocean at incredibly high speed, and the chances of surviving that would be somewhere between minimal and non-existent.

I've watched many of my close friends return from space, and I find the minutes after surviving the re-entry heat until the parachutes deploy to be the hardest part to watch. When I see a capsule plunge through the clouds with no chutes, I always worry they might not appear at all. That's completely terrifying.

Jeremy Hansen arrives on the deck of the USS John P. Murtha after being recovered from the Orion capsule. All four crewmembers were in perfect health after splashdown.

I thought of Catherine and the kids, sending them a "don't worry, gang" message in my mind. Catherine later told me that she had a very bad feeling about the heatshield, so when we emerged from blackout, she began crying and didn't even focus on the parachutes.

Three minutes later, at an altitude of 7,100 metres, timed explosions released small chutes that pulled off the cover for two larger chutes, called drogues because they are intended to slow our acceleration to a speed that would allow our main parachutes to open without ripping. They did their job perfectly, but it was wild inside the capsule, jerking us back and forth like a ride at the fair.

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried.

One minute later, at only 1,500 metres above the ocean, the drogue chutes cut loose, and, for a few moments, we felt like we were falling backward. Then, in succession, the three main parachutes began deploying, blossoming slowly so they wouldn't tear apart. The rate of our fall slowed as the red-and-white nylon canopies, each 35 metres in diameter, filled with air. The thrusters kept firing, aiming the capsule's base directly toward the point of impact.

"Integrity, we see three good-looking parachutes," we heard from our CAPCOM. Within seconds, our splashdown speed had reduced to 27 kilometres per hour.

That's it, I said to myself. I'm pretty sure we can survive whatever else could be thrown at us now.

Christina [Koch, mission specialist] seemed to agree. We grabbed one another's hands in a moment of celebration.

Excerpted from "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, The Groundbreaking Human Mission Into Deep Space" by John Larsen with Jeremy Hansen. © 2026 by John Larsen, used with permission by HarperCollins/Hanover Square Press.

#6472. Eagles may hunt baboons as heavy as some early human relatives

Punctured baboon skulls found beneath cliffs in Chad suggest Verreaux’s eagles may hunt larger primates than scientists once thought possible.

Eagles are known to kill monkeys. A full-grown male baboon, however, has long been considered too heavy for any bird to take.

That view is now challenged by skulls of adult male olive baboons found below desert cliffs in the Sahara. The damage on them suggests that Verreaux’s eagles can kill such animals anyway.

A hole was punched through the bone of the eye socket in each skull. It is the kind of wound that an eagle’s talon leaves. One of the baboons weighed an estimated 48 pounds (21.8 kg).

If the researchers are right, an eagle can kill prey as heavy as some early human relatives.

The study was led by Catherine Hobaiter of the University of St Andrews. She worked with colleagues at Dartmouth College, the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, and African Parks.

No one on the team saw an eagle attack a baboon. The case rests on bones.

Three sites on the Ennedi Plateau were visited by the team in February and March 2025. The plateau is a sandstone landscape in northeastern Chad.

Among the fallen rock below its cliffs, the skulls of two adult male baboons were found at two different sites.

Neither puncture showed signs of healing, so the damage could have occurred around the time of death or afterward.

“We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them,” Hobaiter said.

“Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”

The right shoulder blade of the first male had been punctured and scraped as well. Eagles leave that pattern when they open a body to reach the heart and lungs.

The team also needed to know how heavy the baboons were. The ball at the top of each thigh bone was therefore measured in scaled photographs.

An established formula for monkeys converts that width into an estimate of body weight.

Both thigh bones were found with the first punctured skull. From them, the team estimated that male’s weight at about 48 pounds (21.8 kg).

These weights matter because of a rule of thumb in research on primates and their predators. Primates under 29 pounds (13 kg) are known eagle prey. No heavier primate has ever been confirmed as an eagle’s kill.

Primates between 29 and 44 pounds (13 and 20 kg) are treated as vulnerable in theory. Anything heavier is assumed to be safe from birds.

A third punctured skull was recovered on a return trip in June 2026, along with part of the skeleton. This male weighed an estimated 58 pounds (26.2 kg), and both of his shoulder blades had been scraped.

He was at least twice as heavy as any primate confirmed as eagle prey.

In all, thigh bones were collected from nine baboons. Eight were adult males with an average estimated weight of 49 pounds (22.2 kg).

A hole in a baboon’s skull does not have to come from an eagle. Other causes were therefore considered by the team.

A gunshot would be expected to do much more damage to the skull, and none was found. Male baboons also kill each other with their canine teeth. Such fights tend to leave crushed bone and extra tooth gouges, yet the skulls had neither.

Verreaux’s eagles are known to dive at baboons that come near their nests. No nest was found above or near the skulls, however.

One possibility was harder to dismiss. Verreaux’s eagles sometimes eat dead animals. The scraped shoulder blade could be explained by an eagle pulling apart a carcass.

The authors wrote that this cannot be definitively ruled out. Two reasons to doubt it were given.

First, the skull punctures are far more severe than the shallow pits seen in an earlier experiment. In that experiment, a golden eagle had gripped a dead monkey.

Second, nearly all the bones came from adult males. An eagle that feeds on carcasses would be expected to eat a dead baboon of either sex.

“At first, the idea of eagles hunting adult male baboons seemed to exist on the thin edge of possibility, until it didn’t,” said Nathaniel Dominy of Dartmouth, the study’s senior author.

An eagle does not have to lift its prey to kill it. Golden eagles land on the back of a hoofed animal and hold on until it collapses. Similar methods are used by Verreaux’s eagles.

Verreaux’s eagles also hunt in pairs. The prey is startled by one bird, and the other attacks from below to force it off the cliff.

The grip of a Verreaux’s eagle can span up to 16 inches (40 cm). That is more than twice the width of an adult male baboon’s skull.

The Ennedi baboons appear to spend much of the day on vertical cliff faces. Some are as tall as 490 feet (150 meters).

Water and palm fruit are found on the canyon floor, but it offers little shade or shelter.

When young baboons are threatened by an eagle, the males bark and lunge at it. The team suggested that this could make males more likely to be killed on a cliff.

On June 19, 2026, the researchers watched a pair of Verreaux’s eagles.

The birds flew along a cliff where baboons were resting. Several baboons gave alarm calls, and those in exposed spots dropped quickly to shelter.

“We’d seen them very relaxed around other big birds of prey, but as soon as the Verreaux came into view they alarm called and dropped down to safety,” Hobaiter said.

The argument reaches past baboons because of a famous fossil. In 1995, researchers argued that the Taung Child had been killed by an eagle.

The Taung Child was a young early human relative.

The punctures in the Ennedi skulls resemble the damage to that fossil’s eye socket. The Taung Child, however, weighed an estimated 22 to 26 pounds (10 to 12 kg) at most.

That weight falls inside the accepted limit for eagle prey.

Research on what hunted larger early human relatives has focused on mammals, especially big cats. Hobaiter’s team argued that eagles deserve attention too.

If eagles can kill adult baboons this large, the authors argue that some early human relatives may also have been vulnerable.

Monkeys defend themselves differently against eagles than against cats, and males often step in during eagle attacks.

Several traits could have been shaped by pressure from eagles, the authors wrote. These include the size difference between males and females, cooperation among males, and infant care.

That part of the argument was called speculative by the authors.

Three punctured skulls point to possible eagle attacks, and baboons sounded alarm calls when a pair of Verreaux’s eagles flew past.

The researchers have yet to see one of these eagles attack an adult baboon.

Nearly all the bones came from adult males, and the authors called that pattern puzzling.

3D scans of the bones have been posted in public archives by the researchers, where others can examine the punctures.

Future fieldwork at Ennedi could show whether eagles kill adult male baboons there, and how often.

The full study was published in the journal American Journal of Biological Anthropology.

Ancient writers couldn't agree on how Egypt's last queen took her own life, and the famous snakebite story may owe more to her enemies than to the facts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The death of Cleopatra is among the most famous in history. In 31 B.C., the Egyptian queen and her Roman ally and lover, Mark Antony, lost the Battle of Actium to Octavian, who would later become Rome's first emperor, Augustus. The following summer, Cleopatra was captured during a Roman ambush inside her royal tomb in Alexandria.

According to Octavian’s account, rather than facing the disgrace of defeat, the queen allowed a venomous asp snake to bite her and quickly succumbed to its poison. Some Roman writers, such as the historian Velleius Paterculus, repeated that story without question.

But others were far less certain of this account, calling it Roman propaganda to cement Octavian's rise to power. And most historians today doubt that a snake was involved at all. So how did Cleopatra die?

Live Science spoke with experts, who told us that the queen's death is still shrouded in mystery.

"We cannot know for sure exactly how Cleopatra died," Prudence Jones, a professor of classics at Montclair State University in New Jersey and author of "Cleopatra: A Sourcebook" (University of Oklahoma Press, 2006), told Live Science in an email.

What historians largely agree on is that Cleopatra VII, the last queen of Egypt's Ptolemaic dynasty, took her own life and that she chose a method that left her body composed and dignified.

Physical evidence of Cleopatra's death is elusive. Much of Alexandria's royal quarter now lies underwater, and underwater archaeologist Franck Goddio, who has been excavating it, hasn't found the queen's mausoleum, Jones said. Even if Cleopatra's remains surfaced, bones would be unlikely to show evidence of snake venom, she added, noting that forensics is outside her area of expertise.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Divers celebrate as a crane pulls an artifact from the waters at Abu Qir bay in Alexandria, Egypt on Aug. 21, 2025.

The best witness may have been Olympus, Cleopatra's personal physician. "Unfortunately, nothing survives of Olympus' account," Jones said.

What does remain is a story told largely by Cleopatra's enemies. The earliest surviving account is a poem by the Roman poet Horace, whose patron was a close friend of Octavian, said Jane Draycott, a historian at the University of Glasgow. His Ode 1.37, written around the time of her death, celebrates Octavian's victory and already pictures the queen handling serpents — yet it ends with grudging admiration for a woman who refused to be paraded as a trophy.

Following her capture, Cleopatra was held under military guard. By then, she had already tried to end her life twice. Cleopatra had tried to stab herself when Roman soldiers broke into the mausoleum where she had barricaded herself, and she later tried to starve herself, stopping only after Octavian threatened her children.

To Draycott, those attempts leave little doubt that Cleopatra would rather die than live as a captive. "She does not want to be a prisoner; she does not want to be led through the streets of Rome in triumph as a defeated foe," she told Live Science.

In the Greco-Roman world, suicide didn't carry the stigma it later acquired under Christianity, she added. "It was a way of wiping the slate clean, removing any shame, any disgrace from yourself." After the defeat of his remaining forces at Alexandria and hearing a false report of Cleopatra's death, Antony was the first of the two lovers to die by suicide.

According to the Greek biographer Plutarch, who based his account on that of Cleopatra's personal physician, Cleopatra visited Antony's tomb, bathed, ate and sent Octavian a sealed letter asking to be buried beside Antony, signaling that she meant to die. Octavian realized what was happening and sent messengers rushing to her, but they arrived too late. They found her dead in her royal regalia, with her attendants Iras and Charmion dying beside her.

A statue depicting Cleopatra's suicide by asp, the most famous of several ancient theories.

Jones has compiled what ancient historians, biographers, geographers and physicians wrote about Cleopatra's death. Every source mentions a snakebite, but several also suggest other possibilities, including a poisonous ointment, poison hidden in a hollow hairpin, and snake venom poured into a wound the queen made by biting herself. Only one of these writers, the geographer Strabo, was alive when Cleopatra died, and the only people in the room with her died, too.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio wrote that the sole clue was a pair of faint pricks on her arm. That doesn't settle much, however. "A cobra bite can appear as two small puncture wounds, but not all cobra bites appear this way and not all double puncture wounds result from snakebites," Jones said.

Jones traces the snake version of the story to Octavian, who was in Alexandria when Cleopatra died. Plutarch reported that an image of Cleopatra with an asp clinging to her was carried in Octavian's triumphal procession in Rome. "Octavian, however, was Cleopatra's enemy and for that reason we may not want to accept his account uncritically," Jones said.

Draycott suggested another possible source of confusion: Snake-shaped jewelry was fashionable in Alexandria at the time, so Romans viewing an effigy of the queen may have mistaken a snake bracelet for a real snake.

Draycott doesn't think one snake could have killed all three women. Jones is less certain. Snakes don't inject the same amount of venom with every bite, and some "dry bites" deliver none at all, Jones said. "On the other hand, I don't think it is impossible, as the body of a cobra contains enough venom to kill multiple people," she added.

The general view among historians, Draycott said, is that Cleopatra took some kind of poison — one that worked quickly and didn't cause seizures or vomiting. The absence of these symptoms is telling: An asp is believed to be what is now known as the Egyptian cobra (Naja haje), whose venom causes a slow, agonizing death with respiratory failure.

A young Egyptian cobra (Naja haja) strikes a typical defensive pose in scrubland near Sidi Ifni, Morocco.

Cleopatra likely would have had other means, then. Alexandria was the Mediterranean's center of scientific study, and texts from the period, such as Nicander's "Theriaca," catalog venomous animals, Jones noted. Cleopatra's father, Ptolemy XII, even consulted the pharmacologist Zopyrus about antidotes. Plutarch claimed that Cleopatra personally oversaw experiments that observed the effects of deadly poisons on condemned prisoners.

Still, that claim and other poison stories should be read with caution, Draycott said, because they draw on Roman stereotypes about women. In the Roman view, "manly men will battle with swords," while women, seen as "deceitful and weak" at this time, were thought to kill in secret. "They'll sneak it into your food," Draycott said, summing up the stereotype.

Roman writers were equally suspicious. Poisoning allegations dogged the Hellenistic dynasties of ancient Egypt and the neighboring Seleucid kingdom, as well as Rome's own imperial family. Some were probably true, Draycott said, but others may have been foodborne illnesses or other health conditions people didn't understand.

The method may remain a mystery, but for most historians, the motive doesn't change: Cleopatra chose to die on her own terms.

Olivia is a native Spanish and English speaker.

#6470. Thanksgiving food waste can start before the turkey even goes in the oven

Americans wasted about 166,000 metric tons of food during Thanksgiving week in 2025, roughly 39% more than during a comparison week.

When Thanksgiving food waste comes up, leftovers usually get the blame.

The stuffing went unfinished, or half a pie stayed on the counter until Sunday. In some homes, though, good food is discarded before the meal is even cooked. It is thrown out so a shelf can be cleared for the turkey.

Researchers documented this habit in surveys of U.S. households around Thanksgiving 2025. More edible food was discarded by those households in the holiday week than in a later, ordinary week.

Extra waste was reported by cooks who emptied the fridge to make room. Cooks who had to guess their guests’ appetites reported more too, compared with cooks who made just enough.

The researchers therefore see the days before the meal as a chance to cut holiday waste.

Ran Li of Penn State University and Brian Roe of Ohio State University carried out the surveys. Roe is a professor of agricultural, environmental and development economics.

All of the figures are based on people’s own reports about their kitchens. Nobody’s trash was actually weighed.

“There’s not a lot of great data out there about which holidays cause the most waste,” Roe said. “My money would be on Thanksgiving because it is so focused around the meal – it is the big tradition.”

Household waste surveys normally skip holiday weeks, since researchers are after a typical week. Yearly totals based on such surveys therefore miss the holidays.

For this study, 879 adults were surveyed before and after Thanksgiving 2025. Every one of them handled at least half of the cooking at home.

About a week after the first survey, they reported how much food their households had not eaten. That included anything thrown out, composted or fed to pets.

Bones, peels and pits were left out of the count. Only once-edible food was included.

Later, in December, 437 of the same households repeated the exercise for a non-holiday week.

Households that reported in both weeks discarded about 1.1 pounds (500 grams) of edible food per person during Thanksgiving week.

About 0.8 pounds (358 grams) was discarded in the December week. The Thanksgiving total was therefore 39% higher.

People who skipped the holiday meal discarded about the same amount in both weeks.

The results were then scaled up to the whole country. By the authors’ estimate, Americans discarded about 367 million pounds (166,000 metric tons) of edible food during Thanksgiving week.

That amounts to roughly a pound for every person in the United States.

Based on respondents’ estimates, Americans wasted about $3 billion worth of edible food during Thanksgiving week, roughly 40% more than during the December comparison week.

“That’s a pretty healthy chunk of change, particularly as people are concerned about high food prices right now,” Roe said.

Four out of five respondents took part in a Thanksgiving meal as a host, a guest or both.

About 0.8 pounds (356 grams) per person was discarded that week by people who neither hosted nor attended a meal.

Guests who did not host averaged 1.2 pounds (545 grams). Hosts who did not attend another meal averaged 1.1 pounds (493 grams).

The highest average, 1.8 pounds (818 grams), was reported by respondents who hosted one meal and attended another. That is more than double the amount for people who skipped the holiday.

These gaps remained after age, income, household size and shopping habits were taken into account.

The meal was not blamed for all of that week’s waste. About a quarter of the discarded food was tied by respondents to hosting or attending a Thanksgiving meal.

Different foods were also thrown out by hosts and guests. More meat, turkey included, was discarded by hosts than by guests. Half of the people who only attended a meal had cooked a dish at home to bring.

About 500 respondents cooked for a Thanksgiving meal, either as hosts or as guests bringing a dish. Of those cooks, 74% said they had deliberately made more food than was needed.

The cooks gave three main reasons. Leftovers were the goal for the largest group, 37% of the cooks. Another 25% did not know how much their guests would eat. A further 12% said a big spread was the tradition.

Each of these groups reported more waste than cooks who tried to make just enough. Leftover planners reported about 0.4 pounds (189 grams) more per person for the week.

Cooks who were unsure reported about 0.8 pounds (363 grams) more.

A plan for the extra food was thus associated with less waste than a guess was.

For cooks who guess, tools such as the Guest-Imator were suggested by Li and Roe. It is a calculator from the Natural Resources Defense Council.

A guest count and the amount of leftovers wanted are entered, and the calculator returns quantities to buy.

A use for the extra food was found by many cooks. Among hosts, 37% sent guests home with leftovers. About one in six respondents with leftovers froze some.

The cooks were also asked about the days before the meal. Had food been thrown away to make room for the turkey and the other holiday groceries?

Nearly a pound (438 grams) more waste per person was reported for the week by cooks who cleared space. The comparison was with meal participants who neither cleared space nor cooked too much.

That extra amount alone exceeds the 0.8 pounds reported for the whole week by a person who skipped Thanksgiving.

“They would clear out a bunch of stuff,” Roe said.

Li and Roe wrote that campaigns before the holiday could help. One example they gave was recipes that use up fridge items the night before the turkey is bought.

“Think about what’s in the fridge that can be used up before the turkey’s coming in so that you can have that place for all your fixings for the holiday meal,” he said.

Respondents also reported where the food went: the trash, the compost or the sink.

During Thanksgiving week, 98% more food per person went down the sink or garbage disposal than in December.

Residents of some cities are warned around the holidays about fatbergs. These are buildups of fat, oil and grease that can damage sewer pipes.

The kind of food that went down the drain was not recorded. However, 85% more meat and fish was discarded during Thanksgiving week by households that reported in both weeks.

Li and Roe suspect that holiday cooking adds fat, oil and grease to what goes down the sink.

Because the study is a survey, it shows which habits were associated with more waste. It cannot show that any single habit caused the waste.

The respondents were drawn from an online research panel. Their answers were adjusted to match U.S. households on age, income and household size. Even so, the respondents were not a random sample.

In earlier research, surveys of this kind found 32% to 52% less waste than physical measurement of household waste did. The national totals may therefore be underestimates.

Each household’s waste was also divided by the number of people who normally live there. The number of people at the table was not used. A host’s figure therefore looks bigger, and a guest’s figure looks smaller.

Only about half of the Thanksgiving respondents reported again in December.

For some of them, the December week ended just before Christmas. That week may not have been an ordinary one either.

The survey also did not test any solution. It remains unknown if a portion calculator or a night of use-it-up cooking reduces what is thrown out.

According to Li and Roe, household waste should be weighed over a holiday in future studies.

They also recommended that similar surveys be run for other food-centered holidays.

The full study was published in the journal Waste.

#6469. The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Like parrots, Infernogallus could deftly strip the flesh from large seeds

The ‘hell chicken’ Infernogallus (foreground) dines on Cretaceous fruits, sharing its habitat with a Tyrannosaurus rex (background).

Illustrated by Danielle Dufault, © Danielle Dufault, 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”

Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”

#6468. Offshore wind turbines may reshape the low clouds around them

Clouds can change how much electricity offshore wind farms produce, while turbines can also thin low clouds nearby.

Low clouds over the sea do more than just block sunlight. The tops of these clouds lose heat to space, which cools the air and keeps it moving.

This moving air also affects the wind turbines below.

In computer simulations, turbines in the last rows produced about 11% more power when the air above the clouds was drier than when it was moister.

The wind turbines also affected the clouds. When the clouds were low enough to touch the turbine blades, the turbines made them thinner over several miles in the direction of the wind.

Clouds are left out of many simulations of offshore wind farms.

Researchers at the University of Twente in the Netherlands put them in. Their results suggest that planners of large offshore farms should take clouds into account.

All of this was tested in computer simulations, not at real wind farms.

The clouds in question are stratocumulus. These low, lumpy sheets are the most common cloud type on Earth.

In an average year, they cover about 25% to 30% of the North Sea. Wind energy projects are widespread there, and more are planned.

The North Sea is cloudy so often that its wind farms’ energy output may be affected, said Davide Selvatici. Selvatici is a postdoctoral researcher in the university’s Physics of Fluids group.

Modelers had often worked with idealized skies that held almost no cloud, said Richard Stevens. Stevens is a professor of fluid mechanics at Twente.

Thijs van den Ham, a co-author, said wind farm simulations need clouds in them. “They do play a role, and they do matter,” the author added.

Humidity by itself doesn’t do much to a turbine. Moist air and dry air differ in density by less than 1%. Power output changes by about the same amount.

So the team looked at how clouds change the air’s motion. An earlier study by Selvatici and Stevens had already examined this. In that work, the slowed wind behind a simulated farm recovered faster under low clouds.

The simulations were detailed enough to follow individual gusts and swirls of air.

The work was done in two stages. Cloud layers were first simulated without any turbines, and the temperature and moisture of the overlying air were varied. About 300 simulated hours passed before each of those layers reached a steady state.

A wind farm was then added beneath a selection of those cloud layers. It had 60 turbines in 10 staggered rows, and each was rated at 10 megawatts.

Rotors measured 585 feet (178 meters) across, which put the blade tips 682 feet (208 meters) above the water.

The Washington Monument is shorter than that. At such a height, the blades could reach into the lowest simulated clouds.

A block of air 37 miles (60 kilometers) long surrounded the farm in the model. The block was divided into more than 560 million cells.

Two sets of runs were carried out so that the cloud’s effect could be separated from the effect of moisture.

Cooling at the cloud top was held fixed in the first set. In the second set, cooling was allowed to respond to the moisture overhead, which is how real clouds behave.

When cooling was held fixed, the drier and moister cases differed by about 3% in power from the last rows. A gap that small lies within the uncertainty of the simulations.

Once cooling was allowed to respond, the same comparison produced a difference of 11%.

The cloud itself was responsible for the larger difference, according to the team’s analysis.

Heat is emitted upward by a cloud top, while water vapor in the overlying air radiates heat back down. Less heat is returned by drier air, so the top of the cloud cools more quickly.

That stronger cooling stirred the air underneath more vigorously and the cloud-topped layer deepened. As a result, more of the wind’s energy was transported downward into the farm.

Energy arriving from above is most important at the back of a wind farm.

More than half of the power in the front rows comes from wind that flows in. Each row, however, leaves slower air in its wake for the rows that follow.

In the final rows of the simulated farm, turbulent mixing supplied up to about 90% of a row’s power.

A second effect appeared when the air above the cloud was moister. The cloud-topped layer was then shallower and the approaching wind was slowed more strongly ahead of the farm. The first row of turbines produced less power as a consequence.

Temperature was also found to matter. In the runs with fixed cooling, the researchers varied the temperature contrast between the sea surface and the air above.

The air temperature was taken about 2 miles (3 kilometers) up. The farm’s output then differed by about 20% from a reference case.

Satellite images had already suggested that wind farms affect clouds.

On two mornings, June 5, 2016, and November 14, 2022, North Sea wind farms were photographed by NASA’s Terra satellite. The images showed partly cleared cloud near clusters of wind farms. The team took them from NASA Worldview.

The simulated thinning was strongest under two conditions. The base of the cloud was near the blade tips, and the cloud held little liquid water.

In the run with the lowest cloud, the cloud layer’s top was 587 feet (179 meters) above the sea. That is below the blade tips.

Behind the farm, that cloud held up to 85% less liquid water than in a matching run without turbines.

Warmer, drier air from above was mixed into the cloud by turbulence from the turbines. More of the cloud’s water evaporated.

Ahead of the farm, the cloud changed the opposite way.

The wind slowed as it approached the first row. In that same run, the cloud there held up to about 43% more liquid water than the incoming cloud.

The authors compared that to the Horns Rev wind farm. There, slowing wind ahead of the turbines has been linked to fog forming upwind.

Every run was set in the daytime, with the sun at a fixed angle. Sunlight weakens a low cloud, and the authors wrote that daytime conditions may have amplified the thinning.

The simulations also had no rain, a single farm layout, and the same large-scale wind in every run.

The simulated clouds thinned in the same general way as the photographed ones. The amounts were not compared.

Large clusters of wind farms weren’t simulated either. The authors wrote that those need more observations and more modeling.

Next, the team plans to simulate more kinds of weather and larger farms spaced farther apart. Selvatici noted that simulating real weather conditions will take more computing power than is available now.

The full study was published in the Journal of Renewable and Sustainable Energy.

#6466. At the Races: Regional realignment

New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, New England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.)

One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged New England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a new congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a new congressional map.

California contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Guv update: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Senator Morrison?  Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have launched a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is New Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, new members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”

Ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The New York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

How Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

Was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”

Song of the cycle: The New York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The New York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

If those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

#6465. Even powdery mildew can catch a fungal infection

Researchers found a fungus that infects powdery mildew in preserved specimens, offering clues to how it might help control the crop disease.

Powdery mildew is usually the one doing the damage. The fungi behind it infect crops such as wheat and grapevines, yet some of those mildews are infected themselves, by a fungus called Ampelomyces that lives inside their cells.

Researchers checked dried mildew specimens up to about 150 years old and found the parasite on mildews from many countries.

The study also found that about 13% of the public DNA records labeled Ampelomyces appear to belong to other fungi.

Michael Bradshaw, an assistant professor of entomology and plant pathology at North Carolina State University, led the research with first author Jacklyn Thomas.

Bradshaw directs the university’s Larry F. Grand Mycological Herbarium.

He sees the parasite as a possible tool against the disease. Part of the reason is host specificity, meaning some strains infect only certain kinds of mildew.

“By understanding hyperparasite diversity and how many different strains are out there, it might give us insights on if some are better at controlling the fungus than others,” Bradshaw said.

“There is a degree of host specificity to these hyperparasites, and if we are able to delve deeper they may be very useful in containing this plant disease.”

Powdery mildews include more than 900 species. Together they cause disease in more than 10,000 kinds of flowering plants.

Powdery mildew fungi need living plant tissue to grow, so scientists can’t grow them in lab cultures. That makes their parasite hard to study as well.

So the team turned to herbaria, collections of preserved plants and fungi. The researchers screened 609 mildew specimens held at North Carolina State and at Harvard University’s Farlow Herbarium.

The specimens came from 28 countries, from Argentina and Morocco to Japan and Ukraine. Many reached North Carolina as gifts from herbaria in Germany and Japan.

From each specimen, the team scraped a bit of mildew and tested its DNA for the parasite.

The researchers then checked every positive result under a microscope.

Researchers lifted the mildew onto clear tape and found Ampelomyces under a microscope.

Ampelomyces turned up in 40 of the 609 specimens, or 6.6%. The authors wrote that old collections let them detect a parasite that is hard to observe directly.

Some kinds of mildew were infected far more often than others. Sawadaea mildews had the highest rate, at 14.3%.

Podosphaera and Phyllactinia mildews were among the lowest, at 3.2% and 2.7%.

Some of those groups had only a few specimens, the authors wrote, so small samples may explain part of the spread.

Researchers in Serbia and Hungary, examining field samples under a microscope, had found the parasite in about a third of them.

The detection rate in the herbarium specimens was much lower.

The authors suggested reasons for the gap. Their samples came from many parts of the world, and their DNA tests could miss strains whose genetic code differed from what the tests were built to match.

The team sorted its strains, along with hundreds from public records, by how closely related they were.

Strains from Podosphaera mildews tended to group together, and so did strains from a genus called Arthrocladiella.

Strains from Erysiphe, the largest mildew genus, were scattered across many groups.

The mix of tight groups and scattered strains suggests some Ampelomyces lineages specialize while others infect many kinds of mildew.

Several strains from the herbarium specimens matched no known group and may be new lineages.

One specimen of a mildew called Blumeria showed the parasite under the microscope, but its DNA test failed. The authors suggested that Ampelomyces on Blumeria may be a lineage not yet described.

GenBank is a public database where scientists share DNA sequences. The team downloaded all 671 sequences filed there as Ampelomyces and placed them in one family tree.

Of those sequences, 88 fell outside the main Ampelomyces branch. That is how the team arrived at its estimate that about 13% were probably other fungi.

Even samples from culture collections, which supply living strains to labs, were mislabeled.

One strain listed as Ampelomyces had DNA identical to a fungus called Didymella, though the authors wrote that it may have been contaminated after it left the collection.

Bradshaw said errors like these are a risk whenever researchers rely on large datasets that anyone can add to.

“These parasites are hard to identify, so what happens is someone misidentifies them and enters incorrect data,” he said.

“Then someone else sees that wrong data and uses it to classify their own samples, which leads to more wrong data, and it amplifies that way.”

The team’s answer is a checked reference tree of 47 confirmed strains, posted to a free online tool called T-BAS. Researchers can upload a sequence and see where it belongs.

There are limits. The family tree rests mostly on one short piece of DNA, and its main Ampelomyces branch was only weakly supported.

More genetic data will help sort out how the strains are related, the authors wrote.

Two big questions remain. Are some strains better at fighting the fungus than others?

And did the parasite and the mildew evolve together? Answering the second question will take more samples and whole genomes.

Future research could also expand sampling to more regions and more mildews.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings B.
