#6429. Cattails send oxygen into marsh mud, where it can change the soil chemistry

Cattails grow in mud with almost no oxygen, but their roots bring some in. A new study found that growing roots release oxygen even at night.

The roots of cattails can grow in oxygen-poor marsh mud. To keep these roots alive, the plant carries air down from its leaves.

Part of that oxygen then escapes into the surrounding mud.

It has generally been assumed that this leak occurs mostly in daylight. During the day, the leaves produce oxygen and their pores stay open to the air.

A laboratory study of narrowleaf cattails has found that daylight altered the leak only slightly. Instead, oxygen appeared wherever a new root or underground stem was growing. It remained there through the night as well.

The findings suggest that the season of root growth may matter more for marsh chemistry than the time of day.

The study was conducted by Ilana Stein and Zoe Cardon of the Ecosystems Center. This center is part of the Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL) in Woods Hole, Massachusetts.

Four plants were examined one at a time in boxes of marsh mud. No measurements were made in a marsh itself.

Flooding leaves the soil of a wetland without oxygen. Most wetland plants cope with this through spongy tissue in their leaves, stems and roots that is filled with air.

This tissue serves as a kind of snorkel for the plant. Oxygen travels through it from the air above the water to the root tips below.

Narrowleaf cattail is particularly well adapted to flooded ground. Air spaces were found by earlier studies to make up as much as 74% of its leaf tissue.

In the roots, the figure reached as much as 32%.

Some of the oxygen that arrives is used by the roots and the rest can leak away. This leaked oxygen allows microbes that depend on it to survive in mud where they otherwise could not.

Certain microbes consume methane before the gas can enter the plant and escape through its leaves. Others break down organic matter in the mud and could reduce how much carbon the soil stores.

The same leak is also valuable to people. Cattails are planted in constructed wetlands that treat wastewater and are used to clean up contaminated soil. Both of these uses rely on the oxygen released by their roots.

Cattails and mud were collected by Stein and Cardon from a marsh along the Parker River in northeastern Massachusetts. This marsh forms part of the Plum Island Ecosystems Long Term Ecological Research program.

Each plant was placed in a narrow clear plastic box filled with live mud from the same marsh. The box measured about 15.5 inches tall and 8 inches wide (39 by 20 centimeters).

Much of one inside wall was covered with a film containing a dye that responds to oxygen. A camera photographed the film under blue light.

The colors in every image indicated how much oxygen was present in the mud behind the film.

These films were made by hand by Suzanne Thomas, who works as a senior research assistant at MBL.

Images were captured every few minutes over periods that usually lasted two to three days.

The box itself remained in darkness behind black cloth. Meanwhile, the leaves grew outside under a lamp that was switched on from 5 a.m. to 7 p.m.

A sensor attached to one leaf collected readings once every minute. It recorded how quickly the leaf absorbed carbon dioxide and how widely its pores had opened.

The team could therefore compare the activity of the leaves with the oxygen in the mud.

Mud that held no roots also held no oxygen. This changed as soon as part of a cattail grew into it.

Cattails spread by means of horizontal underground stems known as rhizomes. New roots then emerge from these stems.

Whenever a new rhizome or root entered a patch of mud, the oxygen level there rose rapidly from zero. It climbed to between 25% and 35% of the amount found in water that is fully saturated with air.

This oxygen did not persist for long. Around a rhizome, it disappeared after about three days on average. Around a main root, it lasted about four days.

According to the authors, a seal may be partly responsible. Older sections of a cattail root develop a barrier that is thought to keep oxygen inside. This would allow more of it to reach the growing tip.

Stein and Cardon wrote that this barrier and the steady demand for oxygen in the mud may explain the decline.

In many cases, oxygen returned to the mud a second time. Fine side roots broke through the sealed surface of a main root and oxygen spread through the mud around them.

These later pools of oxygen persisted for about three weeks on average. In one plant, they lasted longer than five weeks.

An earlier study had found that cattail side roots do not develop the barrier that seals a main root.

As a result, a single root released oxygen into the mud on two occasions. The first release lasted a few days near the tip and the second continued for weeks along the sides.

Earlier studies of rice and a salt marsh cordgrass had reported strong control of the leak by day and night. In the cattails, light did have some effect and this was mostly seen around the side roots.

Across three plants, the gap between the highest and lowest oxygen levels of each day averaged about 3% of saturation. No daily pattern could be detected in the fourth plant.

New growth therefore changed oxygen levels far more than the cycle of day and night.

The oxygen in the mud also did not follow the activity of the leaves. It increased during the first two to three hours of light. For the rest of the day, it declined even though the leaves were becoming more active.

After the lights were turned off, the oxygen fell for about two hours. It then rose slowly until the following morning.

Mud consumes oxygen quickly on its own. Oxygen-rich water was injected into mud that held no roots. The oxygen was gone within about an hour and a half.

The roots must therefore have continued to release oxygen in the dark.

The authors wrote that it remains unclear how cattails achieve this without exhausting the oxygen in their own air spaces.

One explanation they proposed is that the leaf pores did not close completely at night. Air could then have continued to enter the plant.

Methane, soil carbon, and microbes were not examined in the study.

The study also followed just four plants of a single species. None of them was kept in its box for more than two months.

If growth is what controls the oxygen, then the next question is when cattails grow underground.

Stein is a postdoctoral researcher in Cardon’s lab. She said the results turned the team’s attention to the timing of root growth across the year.

Earlier field data and models suggest that cattail rhizomes gain the most mass in mid to late summer. This follows the expansion of the leaves.

The authors wrote that oxygen from new rhizomes and their roots may be especially intense during that period.

Methane is released by wetlands naturally and oxygen around roots can reduce it.

“Natural greenhouse gas emissions have been happening forever,” said Cardon, a senior scientist at MBL.

She said the team hopes to identify natural processes that could act as levers on those emissions.

The cattails were not followed through a complete growing season or observed in a marsh. The authors wrote that understanding when rhizomes and roots grow through the year should become a priority.

In their view, such knowledge is needed to understand the chemistry of marshes where cattails dominate.

The full study was published in the journal New Phytologist.

#6428. What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Kratom is a plant, but souped-up products derived from it can have strong and dangerous effects

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

For the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a new set of patients. They show up at the University of Kansas Health System hospital in Kansas City with what looks like severe opiate withdrawal: nausea, vomiting and muscle aches. They’re extremely anxious and sometimes hallucinating. But they haven’t taken an opioid, like fentanyl or heroin. Instead, they’ve used something labeled as kratom, though it may not contain kratom at all.

Kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids. But souped-up new versions with hyperpotent derivatives of the active compound are sold online and in gas stations. The derivatives act strongly on the body’s opioid receptors and are often far more powerful than the opioid drugs they are sometimes intended to replace. Kratom products — sold as pills, liquid shots, edibles and more — are often mislabeled, and state and federal regulations lag far behind.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

A 2026 survey estimated that about 5 million Americans have used kratom or similar products, and the increased use has sent kratom-related exposures up 1,200 percent from only 258 exposures in 2015, according to the National Poison Data System.

Now, newer versions of the substance can produce withdrawal symptoms like nausea and vomiting, which are often so severe they bring people to the hospital. Here’s what to know.

Kratom comes from the dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa, a tree native to Southeast Asia. Dutch scientist Pieter Willem Korthals first described it in 1839. But “without a doubt, it was used likely for centuries prior to that” in countries including Thailand, Indonesia and Myanmar, says Oliver Grundmann, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida in Gainesville. “Wherever there is a stream, these trees are growing there.” People chewed the leaves for a stimulant effect and brewed them into a tea to treat pain,” Grundmann says.

In the United States, kratom is billed pain treatment that is more “natural” than opiates like morphine, Sethi says. “When you take this product at low doses, it is used for waking up … but at higher doses it becomes opiate-like.” Others take it to treat withdrawal or cravings from opioid use.

The leaf form contains more than 40 different naturally occurring chemicals called alkaloids that could have psychoactive effects. The most important is mitragynine, which makes up two-thirds of the plant’s alkaloid content.

Mitragynine acts on the body’s mu opioid receptors. These receptors — found in the brain, spinal cord and gut — usually respond to natural peptide signals in the body such as endorphins, signaling cells to produce pain relief and release chemicals like dopamine. The receptors get their name from the most famous drug that binds to them: opium. Mitragynine is not derived from or related to opium or morphine but it binds partially to the receptor.

“It’s kind of like a dimmer switch versus turning on the lights,” says Mallory Pullman, a clinical toxicologist at the Mississippi Poison Control Center at the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson. “You don’t fully light your room.”

Mitragynine also hits receptors that bind norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine receptors, says Grundmann. The activity at adrenergic receptors creates a stimulant-like effect. “Now I think when we look at mitragynine, it’s primarily kind of this duality of the adrenergic and the opioid receptor activity,” he says, producing stimulating and depressive results in turn.

What nature made, chemists and users are happy to tweak.

As the kratom leaf is dried, Grundmann says, tiny amounts of mitragynine metabolize into another alkaloid, 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH. After someone takes kratom, the body also converts some mitragynine to 7-OH. The small chemical tweak changes the compound from one that binds partially to the mu opioid receptors to one that binds fully — like morphine or opium, Grundmann says. 7-OH binds 10 times more strongly to mu opioid receptors than mitragynine does. The resulting product is far more potent in its effects and addictive potential.

When people use the leaves alone, the amount of 7-OH is extremely limited. But by the mid-2010s, scientists found products with more than 500 percent more 7-OH than in the plant alone, and now, consumers can buy products labeled as pure 7-OH.

While 7-OH can be described as “natural” because it can, in theory, occur in nature, toxicologists like Pullman are also seeing synthetic derivatives that are even stronger, including one molecule named MGM-15. MGM-15 is sold as a “research chemical” and is four times more powerful than 7-OH.

What is in kratom products may not always be what’s on the label, leaving users in the dark about what they are taking. In a 2026 analysis of 44 different kratom products, including tablets, dissolvable films and edibles, Pullman and her colleagues found that 85 percent of the products had contents that did not match the label. Some advertised kratom but contained very high levels of 7-OH. Others had alkaloids that weren’t listed at all.

It’s “very concerning at a consumer level if you can’t trust what’s actually on the label,” Pullman says.

Sethi started hearing the word kratom about 10 years ago in her work with people seeking treatment for opioid use. “I would have patients intermittently tell me about kratom use,” she says. People were using kratom to stay off opioids, or to treat pain, and didn’t report being addicted to the plant.

Patients who started using kratom or 7-OH to get off opioids “now are having really bad withdrawal and cravings and ending up in the hospital,” she says. Some are seeking addiction treatment, not for opioids, but for kratom and 7-OH. In 2025, U.S. poison centers documented 3,434 kratom-related exposure reports, reported both by people who called the center and medical professionals. “I see less fentanyl and more kratom at this point, or more 7-OH,” Sethi says.

In July of 2026, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily classified some kratom derivatives as Schedule I drugs, meaning they have high abuse potential and no medical use. Those derivatives include 7-OH and another related kratom derivative, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl or MGPI, as well as MGM-15 and its powerful sibling MGM-16. The DEA re-upped the temporary scheduling of MGM-15 and 16 and MGPI in October. 7-OH was temporarily placed in Schedule I at any dose higher than that found in the kratom plant. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has also issued statements warning consumers not to use the products. None of these measures affect the legality of the kratom leaf itself.

Regulations vary at the state level: Twenty-six states don’t regulate kratom at all, while six states and the District of Columbia list kratom’s ingredients as a Schedule I controlled substance, like the current federal scheduling. A further 18 states regulate sale and manufacture in some way.

“I think there’s a lot more concern now, especially that there might be potential opioids out on the market,” Pullman says. Regulations are trying to thread the needle between banning the plant and banning high-potency derivatives, knowing that when one derivative gets smacked down, another will quickly appear in its place. That cycle is a familiar one, mirroring the evolution and development of synthetic opioids.

“There’s risk with everything,” she says. “I think it’s important to distinguish the difference between a synthetic product versus the natural, and that way we can clearly attribute where the risk lies.”

#6427. Fatal cases of Ebola often share a striking pattern

Ebola may trap immune messages inside infected cells, keeping the body's defenses active longer and potentially worsening illness.

A deadly virus such as Ebola might be expected to kill by shutting down the body’s defenses.

Ebola virus does make proteins that block a key signal the body uses to fight infection. The pattern in patients, however, is the opposite.

People who die from Ebola often show the highest activity in the genes that fight viruses.

Scientists have struggled to explain this for years.

A new study points to the tiny droplets of protein and RNA that Ebola virus builds inside infected cells. These droplets are known as viral condensates, and the cell’s own immune messages become trapped inside them.

Once trapped, the messages are not broken down when they should be.

The defense therefore remains switched on. That prolonged response may be part of what makes patients so ill.

The findings come during a major outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

As of November 17, the CDC reported 11,613 confirmed cases and 5,678 confirmed deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The outbreak involves Bundibugyo virus, a close relative of the virus studied here.

Two of them make proteins called NP and VP35. Both attach to viral RNA and to each other, gathering into droplets that have no outer membrane.

During an infection they can take up between one-fifth and one-third of a cell.

Jingru Fang led the work in the Saphire Lab at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology. Fang now works at Princeton University’s Omenn-Darling Bioengineering Institute.

“When birds land in a new place, they make nests where they can raise their babies,” said Fang.

“You can imagine viral condensates as nests for a virus.”

To study the droplets, NP and VP35 were introduced into human kidney cells. The actual virus was left out, and the droplets still formed.

The messenger RNA in those cells was then stained. Messenger RNA carries the instructions a cell uses to make a protein.

Messenger RNA was more concentrated inside the droplets than in the surrounding cell fluid.

In human cells, the buildup came to roughly 40%. Kidney cells from Egyptian fruit bats showed an even greater buildup.

When NP was changed so that it could no longer attach to single-stranded RNA, that buildup fell by about half.

A similar change to VP35 had little effect in human cells. NP appears to play the bigger role in collecting RNA.

That figure covers every message at once, and says nothing about which ones are collected.

The team therefore used a method capable of reading thousands of RNA types at once, across 136 genes linked to Ebola infection and the immune response.

About 90,000 cells were examined, with droplets found in roughly 30% of them. Of the 66 genes measured reliably, all but two were more concentrated inside.

The amount of RNA made little difference. Rare messages collected inside while far more common ones stayed out, indicating that something other than abundance determined where they ended up.

Shape proved to be the better explanation.

RNA is not always a straight strand. Parts of it join together wherever the letters match, folding the molecule into loops and stems.

Messages with fewer folds in their protein-making sections entered more readily.

To test this, the genetic instructions in some messages were rewritten. The new versions made the same protein but folded differently, and those with fewer folds entered more readily.

Ten viruses that carry negative-strand RNA were also examined, including Ebola, measles, rabies and Marburg. In all of them the protein-making regions had fewer folds than the human messages left outside.

The most striking finding concerned interferon. Type I interferon, released when a cell detects a virus, switches on hundreds of defense genes in nearby cells.

After the cells were treated with interferon, the droplets started collecting different messages.

Messages from more than 20 defense genes appeared in droplets.

The rule governing entry also changed. The protein-making section was no longer the best indicator.

Instead the tail of each message mattered more, the stretch that follows the instructions for making a protein.

Immune defense messages often have long, tightly folded tails.

The more folded the tail, the more of that message was found inside. Interferon also increases proteins that attach to RNA, and some of these may help pull immune messages into the droplets.

People who die from Ebola often show stronger activity in their defense genes than those who survive. Even people who recover can show signs of inflammation-related gene activity years later.

Erica Ollmann Saphire, who led the study with Fang, is the president and chief executive of the La Jolla Institute for Immunology.

“These are strong immune responses, but they’re not working well,” said Ollmann Saphire.

Cells normally break down messenger RNA once it has served its purpose. Enzymes such as XRN1 help carry out that cleanup.

Staining showed less XRN1 inside the droplets than in the surrounding cell fluid.

This raised a further question: whether messages trapped inside survive longer because the enzymes cannot reach them.

Messages held in the droplets broke down more slowly than the same messages in cells carrying a modified NP that could not bind RNA. Messages that stayed outside broke down at similar rates in both groups.

“The antiviral response is like a weapon, and cells use degradation as a way to deactivate that weapon,” Fang explained.

Protein production also changed. A protein the cell requires in order to start building other proteins was largely missing from the droplets.

Without interferon, more messenger RNA collected inside but less protein came out of it.

With interferon, both rose: one defense message increased more than sixfold, and levels of two defense proteins rose alongside it.

A final experiment used a weakened Ebola virus, one lacking a gene needed for replication.

A defense message called IFIT3 was found inside the droplets of those infected cells as well.

Bats can carry filoviruses without getting sick. These viruses belong to the same family as Ebola.

Bat genes cannot be read with tools designed for human RNA. Computer models were therefore used to predict how 45 of the collected messages would fold, in bats, ferrets and macaques.

Ferrets and macaques can become seriously ill from Ebola, which makes them useful comparisons.

Within the defense genes, the bat versions had tails that were less tightly folded than the human ones. Ferret and macaque tails were much more like those in humans.

Genes outside the defense group showed no meaningful difference between species.

Fever often comes with an interferon response, so the predictions were repeated at 102 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius).

Messages carrying bat tails then behaved as the folding had predicted. The least folded bat tail kept its message out of the droplets better than the matching human tail.

Bat immune messages may therefore be less likely to become trapped. If they remain outside, cells can break them down at the usual time.

Most experiments used kidney cells grown in a laboratory. The process was not tested in human patients or living animals, and for much of the work NP and VP35 stood in for the complete virus.

The cells were measured at just one point, 24 hours after the proteins were introduced, across 136 genes out of roughly 20,000.

The human kidney cells responded poorly to interferon. Higher concentrations were therefore used for longer periods than other tissues might need.

The RNA folding patterns were computer predictions. They cannot fully show how every RNA molecule behaves inside a living cell.

The bat comparison included only one species. It was chosen partly because scientists have not yet identified Ebola virus’s natural host.

“We don’t know whether this difference can explain everything, but it gives researchers a place to start looking and confirm what we’ve found in additional human or animal samples,” Fang added.

Breaking the droplets apart may be worth pursuing as a treatment, the authors wrote. It could slow the virus and prevent immune messages from remaining active too long.

The principal challenge is achieving that inside living cells without destroying the cells.

The full study was published in the journal Cell.

Physicists at the Large Hadron Collider have detected a rare, 1-in-10-billion particle interaction that opens a view into the 'zeptoverse,' the smallest distance scale ever measured.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Using the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's largest particle accelerator, scientists have gotten the first glimpse of the "zeptoverse" — the universe as it behaves within less than a hundred-trillionth of a wavelength of visible light, the smallest scale that researchers have explored to date.

The new findings may one day help to answer long-standing cosmic mysteries, such as why there is far more matter than antimatter seen in the universe, and what makes up the dark matter that constitutes about 85% of all matter in the universe, the researchers announced Nov. 3 at a seminar at CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research), the organization that operates the LHC. The study, available as a preprint, has not yet been peer reviewed.

At the LHC, located near Geneva at the border of France and Switzerland, researchers were investigating elusive particles called beauty quarks. These subatomic particles are cousins of the standard "up" and "down" quarks that make up the cores of all atoms in the universe.

When beauty quarks are created — in this case, when the LHC smashes atoms together at incredibly high speeds — they live for just one and a half trillionths of a second before they decay. There are a number of ways beauty quarks can break down; researchers hope that analyzing rare forms of these decays might reveal that they might not unfold as expected.

Such outcomes could then shed light on new kinds of physics found only at very tiny scales of zeptometers, or trillionths of a nanometer. (For comparison, a wavelength of visible light ranges from about 380 to 750 nanometers.)

An artist's visualization of a beauty particle decaying into two muons.

By exploring this zeptoverse, scientists hope to discover new particles that have escaped detection until now.

"We're confident there must be new particles to discover, and these could help explain mysteries like dark matter and the existence of matter in the universe," study co-author Harry Cliff, a particle physicist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Why haven't we seen these particles yet? One answer, and perhaps the most likely answer, is these new particles only become manifest at very, very short-distance scales. So by probing into the zepto scale, we give ourselves the best chance possible of finding these new particles that could explain these mysteries."

We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past.

Now, after hunting for more than four decades, physicists have found the first evidence of the rarest kind of beauty-quark decay seen yet. "Only one in 10 billion beauty particles decay this way," Cliff said.

In this form of decay, technically known as the B0 to mu+ mu− decay, a beauty quark collides with an oppositely charged beauty antiquark. They annihilate each other, generating a pair of smaller particles ‪—‬ a muon and an antimuon. Previous research suggested that this requires a complicated set of interactions, making this kind of decay extraordinarily rare.

An experiment at the LHC called LHCb was specifically designed to study beauty quarks. In 2024, a major upgrade to LHCb made it possible to distinguish different types of particles. Using machine learning techniques, the researchers suppressed huge amounts of background noise, which helped them detect the first evidence of the B0 to mu+ mu− decay.

"We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past," Cliff said. "And so we have this massive sample of beauty decays, and that is ultimately what allowed us to see this decay for the first time."

The new results suggest that the way this rare decay happens matches the predictions of the Standard Model of particle physics, the current best description of how the basic building blocks of the universe behave. As such, the researchers have not yet discovered signs of new particles or new physics beyond the Standard Model.

"For me, I think the most exciting thing about this result is the fact that we are probing these unimaginably short distance scales," Cliff said. "Seeing the evidence for this decay begins a new area of research where we can start to make precision measurements that will give us the best chance of finding new physics in the future."

The researchers would now like to upgrade LHCb to fully exploit the improvements to the LHC's luminosity that are currently planned for the 2030s.

"However, there is some doubt over that now because the U.K. recently withdrew funding from the project," Cliff said. "So we are really trying to figure out if we'll be able to continue this type of research."

In an ideal world, "we'll collect many hundreds of these decays in the future, make precise measurements and probe deep into the zeptoverse," Cliff said.

#6424. Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.

Meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group. How well can one find its way alone?

In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.

After release, 18 reached a familiar spot or found their group. Fourteen headed first to the burrow where the group had slept.

The team found no clear advantage for older or more experienced animals.

The researchers suggest that daily group travel may give meerkats enough experience to navigate alone.

The study was led by Mathilde Martin of the University of Zurich. The team worked alongside the Kalahari Meerkat Project, which follows about 15 wild groups accustomed to people.

The project is run from the Kalahari Research Centre, which is known as the KRC.

“At the KRC, our work with meerkats allows us to distract them with a water bottle and fit their collar in a few seconds while they stand upright drinking; a mere formality for them,” Martin said.

A GPS tag on each collar logged the position of the animal once every second. A radio transmitter was also fitted, along with a small audio recorder for the meerkat’s calls.

The team tested a total of 20 adults from five groups between January and March 2025. Fifteen of these animals were male, whereas only five of them were female.

Each meerkat was caught while its group was foraging and was released up to 0.9 miles (1.5 kilometers) away.

Such a distance is greater than the ground usually covered by a meerkat group in a whole day.

The release sites were located inside the territory of each group. The team chose areas that the group had not visited for at least 30 days.

Homing experiments of this kind have previously been carried out on honeybees and desert ants. Highly social animals that travel in tight groups have rarely been tested in the same way.

This is because the knowledge of one animal is difficult to separate from the decisions of the group.

Eighteen of the 20 meerkats left the release site. The sleeping burrow, the capture spot or the group itself was reached by all 18 of them.

Some of the meerkats departed almost at once, whereas others circled the release site for nearly 90 minutes.

The area covered by them ranged from half an acre to almost 17 acres (2,050 to 68,200 square meters).

A meerkat rarely strayed from its course once a direction had been chosen. Sixteen of the animals aimed for a fixed place.

The sleeping burrow was visited first by 14 of those 16.

On average, the straight-line distance to the target amounted to 82% of the distance actually walked by the meerkat.

The release areas had not been visited by the group for a month. The team therefore concluded that the meerkats had been navigating from long-term memory.

Two males never left the release site, and they were carried back to their groups after 90 minutes. They were no younger or less experienced than the others.

The authors suspect that stress kept them there, and not a lack of knowledge.

Some meerkats had been expected to navigate better than others. Subordinate males sometimes leave the group and go alone in search of mates.

Other females are occasionally driven out for a while by the dominant female.

Solo trips of this kind could be counted as practice. The researchers also considered the age of each animal, together with the time it spent on guard duty.

Attention was given as well to how often it scent-marked the territory or dug at shelters.

None of those traits predicted how long a meerkat explored. Neither did they predict how accurately it set off or how straight it travelled.

No clear difference was found between males and females either, although only five females took part.

The authors think that the explanation lies in the territory itself. It is small and stable, with 0.3 to 0.6 miles (0.5 to 1 kilometer) covered by a group daily.

The whole territory has probably been crossed several times by each member by the time adulthood is reached.

The authors wrote that pigeons of different ages are likewise able to find their way home equally well.

On the way home, the meerkats spent about two-thirds of their time searching for cues. Most of the remaining time was spent moving.

Few of them stopped to eat, and those that did only grabbed millipedes crawling on the sand.

The animals stood upright or climbed a bush or tree trunk in order to scan the landscape. Overall, they spent 10 times longer on looking than on sniffing.

This balance between looking and sniffing was altered late in the trip. By that stage, a meerkat had reached its target and was searching for its group. Sniffing then took up more than 20% of its cue-searching time.

Along the way, meerkats were often seen sniffing around boltholes. These are the small shelters that the animals dig across their territory. An earlier experiment had found that meerkats remember where their boltholes are.

The authors suggested that boltholes may serve as landmarks in a meerkat’s memory of its territory.

The search was not ended by reaching the burrow, because the group could have moved on since the capture.

Thirteen of the 20 meerkats rejoined their groups on their own. The slowest took almost three hours.

The burrow or the capture site was reached by five others. The group had nevertheless not been found by them when the three-hour limit ran out.

These animals were caught again and returned by the team.

The researchers could not explain why some meerkats succeeded while others did not. Success was not predicted by a straighter trip to the burrow.

Nor was it predicted by the number of scent marks left behind by the group.

The tracking of a group was compared by the authors to a predator following its prey. The target keeps moving and its route is not known to the searcher.

Twenty animals make up a small sample, as the authors wrote. All of them were subordinate adults older than 10 months, so pups and dominant animals were not tested.

Every release was also made inside familiar territory. The results therefore do not show how a meerkat would manage in a place it does not know.

Two reasons for looking around could not be fully separated either. A lone meerkat that scans the landscape may be checking for predators as much as searching for landmarks.

If many group members know the territory, the next question is who leads when the group moves.

The authors want to know whether certain traits influence which animal takes the lead. The physical needs of an animal and its social rank are two examples.

Co-author Benjamin Robira said the team now wants to understand what makes up a meerkat’s mental picture of its territory.

The researchers also intend to study how the animals get from one point to another.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

#6423. Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

#6421. Rainforest ferns from an ancient lineage have a surprisingly young family tree

An ancient lineage of rainforest ferns reveals how rising mountains and retreating wetlands may have shaped plant diversity across tropical America.

Some rainforest ferns belong to a lineage that stretches back to the age of dinosaurs. Yet roughly half its living species arose within the past six million years, as mountains rose and landscapes changed.

Researchers at the University of Turku and Aarhus University have reconstructed the history of tropical American Danaea ferns.

The findings draw on decades of work identifying ferns and establishing where they grow. That groundwork made it possible to investigate how the group spread and diversified.

“We have conducted extensive research at the University of Turku in order to understand the biodiversity of the Amazon rainforest,” said senior author Hanna Tuomisto, a professor of ecology.

“In the last 25 years, we have discovered and described 47 new Danaea species previously unknown to science, and have clarified the distribution and phylogenetic relationships of the species in the Danaea genus.”

“We have now been able to link this information to the geological and climatic history of tropical America.”

The team combined DNA evidence from 78 species with 2,289 verified records of where the ferns grow. These records helped reconstruct where ancestral ferns probably lived and the elevations they occupied.

The genetic analysis included 11 species that had not yet been formally described.

The researchers’ preferred estimate suggests that the Danaea lineage split from the lineage of its closest living relatives about 128 million years ago, during the Early Cretaceous.

The common ancestor of its surviving species lived much later, around 53 million years ago. The researchers traced that ancestor to Amazonia.

But an ancient lineage need not consist of ancient species. About half of today’s Danaea species originated during the past six million years.

This complicates a familiar explanation for tropical richness: favorable conditions allowed species to accumulate over immense stretches of time.

Persistence mattered, but the landscape also kept changing, creating opportunities for new species.

Fern diversity generally reaches its greatest heights in tropical mountain forests. Danaea follows a different pattern: Amazonia has consistently held its largest pool of species in the reconstruction.

“Mountain rainforests are home in particular to an abundance of epiphytes – plants that grow on top of other plants. Danaea ferns, on the other hand, grow on the forest floor,” said lead author Venni Keskiniva, a postdoctoral researcher at Turku.

“These research results are, in fact, similar to those obtained for trees, which are also the most species-rich in lowland rainforests.”

Where a plant lives within a forest may therefore help explain where its group becomes most diverse. Findings from one fern group cannot automatically describe them all.

The Andes still played an important role. Although Amazonia contained more species, the mountains became the leading source of dispersal to other regions.

Mountain formation affected far more than the slopes themselves. As the Andes rose, they changed rainfall patterns along with the soils developing across neighboring lowlands.

Vast wetlands once occupied much of western Amazonia. Their drainage near the end of the Miocene opened additional land for forest plants to colonize.

The resulting western Amazonian soils were generally richer in nutrients and more variable, than soils in central Amazonia.

Those differences may have encouraged plants to specialize in different environments.

The timing fits the fern history. Most new Amazonian species arising within the past six million years appeared in western Amazonia during the last three million.

New land in southern Central America also offered room for expansion. Arriving lineages frequently gave rise to additional species as the region’s landscapes developed.

The first mountain-adapted Danaea lineages appeared around 20 million years ago, following an intensification of Andean uplift. Several later spread into regions farther from the equator.

Their earlier move uphill may have helped them cope with the conditions they encountered there.

“As the plants had already adapted to the cooler climate of the mountains, it may have been easier for them to spread to areas where the temperature differences between the seasons are greater,” Keskiniva said.

Lineages that remained adapted to Amazonian lowlands tended to stay within that region.

The repeated sequence of mountain colonization followed by expansion suggests that climate tolerance influenced which routes were available.

The mountains could both separate populations and help others reach new habitats. Their role changed as the landscape rose and different fern lineages established themselves.

Assigning dates to this history was difficult. Many relevant fossils are fragmentary, and researchers disagree about where they belong in the family tree.

The team compared three dating approaches, which produced substantially different ages. It favored the reconstruction most consistent with other biological and geological evidence.

The dates remain estimates, and coinciding events do not establish a cause by themselves. Still, the findings connect the survival of ancient lineages with much younger episodes of diversification.

“The biodiversity in rainforests is the result of a long history, but its formation has also been greatly influenced by events that are relatively recent on a geological time scale,” Keskiniva concluded.

The study is published in the journal Frontiers of Biogeography.

#6420. The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The virus, eliminated in 2000, has now been circulating for more than a year

Flyers provide information about a Pennsylvania Department of Health measles vaccination clinic in Lancaster County aiming to curb an ongoing outbreak.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.

The highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17. Analyses of cases dated from when the first outbreak began in 2025 in West Texas through part of 2026 revealed the virus has been spreading uninterrupted for more than a year. That benchmark signals measles is no longer under control.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The United States is not alone. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status, PAHO announced; Canada had lost it in 2025. “Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage,” PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa said in a Nov. 17 news conference. “And this global trend is also affecting the Americas.” Countries will need to not only stop ongoing outbreaks, but also prove that no one caught measles within their borders for a full year to regain measles-free status.

That won’t happen overnight. But there is a way, experts say. Vaccinating people across the country, particularly in areas with low vaccination rates, will stifle the virus’s spread. But so far, the U.S. federal public health response has taken a back seat to efforts from state and local health departments to curb ongoing outbreaks.

Measles’s return “is an enormous black eye on the reputation of the United States,” said epidemiologist Jennifer Nuzzo of the Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I., in a Nov. 9 webinar hosted by the university. The Americas led the global campaign to control the virus, and in 2016 the region became the first to eliminate measles transmission from all its countries.

“To lose [elimination status] means we’re going backwards… meaning decades of progress lost,” Nuzzo said. “It’s an indicator of our lack of protection. It is an indicator of our lack of preparedness for disease threats in general.”

PAHO’s verdict comes amid a surge of measles not seen in the United States since 1991. Health officials have recorded more than 7,000 cases since the beginning of the West Texas outbreak. That tally includes nearly 2,300 measles cases in 2025 and 5,412 in 2026 as of November 12, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over 90 percent of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated or whose status is unknown. States report that 13 people have died, although the CDC so far recognizes only nine of those deaths.

While mild measles symptoms include high fever, cough and a rash, roughly 1 in 5 people will be hospitalized with complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Children younger than 5 years and adults over 20 are more likely to get sick, as are pregnant women and their infants. At least 13 babies were born infected, called congenital measles, since the beginning of 2025, researchers report November 16 in NEJM Evidence. Those babies are at risk for developing dangerous brain swelling that is almost always fatal later on in life.

The measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine helped eliminate measles from the United States in 2000. After that, cases still sometimes popped up. Those cases were mostly in unvaccinated people traveling from parts of the world where the virus still widely circulates. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

But widespread misinformation, including a disproven claim that the vaccine causes autism, means fewer children are receiving the MMR shot and more people are questioning its safety. According to the CDC, roughly 92 percent of kindergarteners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019. And in 2025, 83 percent of U.S. adults viewed the MMR vaccine as safe, down from 86 percent in 2024, according to a survey from the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. Yet decades of evidence show the vaccine is safe and highly effective.

That measles made a comeback is not a surprise, says Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University School of Medicine. Until recently, outbreaks were largely isolated to communities with low vaccination rates and quickly contained. But now, outbreaks seem to be more likely to spill over into neighboring communities, Lo says. “There’s a lot of potential connectedness between the outbreaks.”

What’s more, some infected people aren’t getting tested, making them invisible to officials who are now struggling to trace chains of transmission. An outbreak that hit Arizona and Utah, for instance, was far larger than official numbers suggest, researchers reported July 15 in a preprint at medRxiv.org. The roughly 1,000 confirmed cases may represent just 20 to 30 percent of the outbreak’s true size.

A functional surveillance system is crucial to keeping outbreaks under control, Jonathan Temte, a family medicine physician at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, said in the Brown University webinar. Without good surveillance across the entire country, “we can miss pockets out there if people aren’t reporting, if people are hiding cases.”

But surveillance alone won’t stop the virus from “popcorning across the country,” Nuzzo said. “Measles has returned, and it’s going to take vaccination to stop it.”

Over the last two years, measles outbreaks have popped up across the United States, sickening thousands of people since mid-January 2025. Most of those cases, shown by county where they were reported, are in people who are unvaccinated. Colors on the map indicate the relative number of cases reported. Green represents the lowest and red the highest number of cases. Notable outbreaks have appeared in Utah, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

Michael Mitchell and Andrea Uhlig/Brown University School of Public Health

Efforts to boost vaccine uptake could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles, but not all. “Figuring out which ones are [high risk] can be a little tricky,” Lo says. “But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

Homing in on school districts or individual schools could also help. State health departments typically report vaccination rates among school-age children by county. But that broad metric can hide high risk schools with low vaccination rates, epidemiologists Siyu Chen and Ana Bento reported in August in Nature Medicine. Computer simulations relying on data that included 50,000 schools across the United States showed that school-level estimates best revealed where the virus could gain a foothold. That was true even if county-level vaccination rates were close to 95 percent.

Another element that influenced where measles took off was whether communities with cases were near other areas with low vaccination rates, the team found. The outbreak in Texas, for instance, may have ended faster because communities with low vaccination rates were farther away from one another compared with outbreaks in South Carolina and Pennsylvania, says Bento, of Cornell University. Neighboring areas where many are unvaccinated may face longer-burning outbreaks. “Which is what we are now seeing,” Bento says.

Measles elimination status can be regained. The declaration that the virus is endemic is “not a punishment,” Bento says. It’s a sign that something needs to change. That might include vaccine catch-up campaigns, community outreach or getting rid of nonmedical vaccine exemptions.

Local public health officials are “doing every last thing that you can imagine with limited resources,” health psychologist Noel T. Brewer said in a Nov. 12 webinar hosted by the Association of Health Care Journalists. But a cohesive plan at the federal level could bolster defenses before the virus arrives in new states, noted Brewer, of the University of North Carolina Gillings School of Global Public Health in Chapel Hill.

Such efforts could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles. “A subset [with low vaccination rates] are high risk,” Lo says. “Figuring out which ones are which can be a little tricky. But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

There’s also wiggle room in the childhood vaccine schedule to provide kids extra protection. Normally children don’t get their first MMR dose until their first birthday. But doctors can give infants an extra MMR dose at 6 months if there is an active outbreak in their area. Pediatricians can also offer the second dose a month after the first one, rather than waiting until around the time children start kindergarten. Adults, particularly those who received only one dose, can also get a booster. It’s unclear whether health officials will officially recommend such actions.

“The problem is that there’s no trusted source for this vaccine decision anymore,” Lo says. Previous vaccine recommendations were up to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which was disbanded in March after lawsuits blocked appointments made by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Now, there’s a lot of different medical societies and initiatives to try and fill that void,” Lo says. But it’s unclear which would be best positioned to lead.

CDC director Erica Schwartz has said the health agency will not be changing its response to ongoing outbreaks. “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” she told Reuters. The CDC did not respond to Science News requests for an interview, but shared in a Nov. 17 statement that the agency will “encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”

Eliminating measles again will take dedicated resources and more funding funneled to public health departments across the country, Lo says. “You see increasing measles outbreaks and a lot of time and resources to contain these outbreaks at a time where you’re slashing budgets,” Lo says, “that’s a really bad mismatch.”

Public health responses to measles are expensive. Officials in New Mexico spent an estimated $5.4 million — over $53,000 per case — responding to a 2025 outbreak that was linked to West Texas. The CDC has provided an additional $100 million to states to help fight measles.

Other countries have beaten back measles after an unwelcome return. Extensive vaccination campaigns helped Venezuela and Brazil regain measles elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019. The Public Health Agency of Canada also announced that its nearly two-year-long outbreak officially ended in October, though it’s unclear when the country might earn its status back.

“It is not hopeless,” Nuzzo said. “It can be done, and I hope it will be done [in the United States].”

#6419. Even slightly warmer summers are linked to a higher death risk for people with heart disease

A UK study links extreme heat and repeated heatwaves to higher death risks among people with heart disease.

An average summer temperature of about 62°F (16.5°C) sounds mild. But even slightly warmer summers were linked to a higher risk of death among people with cardiovascular disease.

In a large UK study, researchers found that for every 1.8°F (1°C) increase in average summer temperature, patients had a 15% higher risk of dying from any cause.

The risk was also higher among patients who experienced more heat waves. The odds of death rose on the hottest days and after sharp jumps in temperature from one day to the next.

Taken together, the findings indicate that heat may influence survival across entire seasons in heart patients. An influence during brief hot spells is suggested as well.

The research was conducted by Ka Yan Lai of the University of Hong Kong alongside colleagues there. Further collaborators were based at the University of Oxford.

Using health records, the investigators followed nearly 64,000 UK patients for periods of up to 16 years.

Lai said the health effects of extreme heat have “rarely been studied among people with pre-existing conditions.”

All of the patients had been enrolled in UK Biobank, a long-running British health project. Half a million volunteers aged between 37 and 73 were recruited to it from 2006 to 2010.

From this pool, 63,860 volunteers were selected by the team for analysis.

All received their first hospital diagnosis of cardiovascular disease between 2006 and 2022.

Cardiovascular disease, or CVD, includes conditions that affect the heart and blood vessels.

Four of those disorders were examined on their own as well. Atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat, was the first of them.

The second was ischemic heart disease, in which narrowed arteries can’t deliver enough blood to the heart. Heart failure and stroke made up the remaining two.

At diagnosis, the patients had reached an average age of about 69 years. Deaths from any cause had been recorded for 12,237 of them by the end of 2022.

That figure corresponds to roughly one patient in five.

Temperature data were taken from the daily records kept by the Met Office. Those records are mapped onto squares measuring about 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) across.

For every summer, defined as June through August, each home address was matched to its square.

Considerable variation in average summer temperature was evident across that map. The coldest squares averaged about 43°F (6.1°C), whereas the warmest reached about 66°F (18.7°C).

The central result relates to the average summer temperature at each patient’s place of residence. A 15% higher risk of death was associated with every additional 1.8°F (1°C).

Several other influences had been accounted for before that estimate was produced. Among them were age, sex, smoking, alcohol use, diabetes and neighborhood deprivation.

For patients with ischemic heart disease, each added degree Celsius corresponded to a 19% higher risk. A smaller increase of 10% was found among those with atrial fibrillation.

The results for heart failure and stroke were less certain. In both groups, the link with average summer temperature was too weak to exclude chance.

Adults aged 65 and older in New England had been examined in an earlier US study.

A 1% increase in deaths was reported there for each 1.8°F (1°C) rise in long-term average summer temperature. Older adults in general were covered by that work, not only people with heart disease.

Heat waves were also counted by the researchers. A heat wave was defined as two or more consecutive days hotter than 90% of local summer days.

Exposure to four or more heat waves a year was experienced by some patients. Their risk of death exceeded by 24% that of patients exposed to two or fewer.

Among patients with atrial fibrillation, the corresponding increase in risk was 29%. It stood at 28% among those with heart failure.

A second analysis was restricted to patients whose deaths occurred during a summer.

For each such patient, temperatures on the day of death and the five preceding days were examined. These were then compared with other days in the same month that fell on the same weekday.

Because every patient served as their own comparison, fixed traits can’t account for the results. Sex and schooling are examples of such traits.

On the hottest 1% of summer days, the odds of death among the patients as a group were 70% higher. The reference point was the temperature at which deaths were lowest.

Temperature changes from one day to the next were measured as well. The largest one-day rises were taken to be those in the top 1% of such changes.

After rises of that size, the odds of death were roughly double those seen when temperature held constant.

Roughly threefold odds were found in patients with ischemic heart disease or heart failure.

Considerable uncertainty surrounds the estimates for sharp rises. In heart failure, the plausible range extended from 36% higher odds to more than seven times as high.

No clear link with deaths was detected for sudden drops in temperature.

Events inside the patients’ bodies were not measured at any point in the study. A plausible explanation was instead drawn by the authors from earlier research on extreme heat.

In hot weather, warm blood is pumped toward the skin so that heat can be shed by the body. As much as 5 gallons (20 liters) of blood may be pumped by the heart each minute.

Sweating can meanwhile strip water and salt from the body. Blood that holds less water becomes thicker, and thicker blood may clot more readily.

In a person with heart disease, the extra pumping may require more oxygen than the heart can obtain.

Among patients lacking a college or university degree, warmer summers were tied more strongly to death. A weaker link was seen in patients who held such a degree.

A similar contrast emerged between neighborhoods with moderate green space and the greenest neighborhoods, where the link was weaker.

Among heart failure patients, the link was stronger in the most deprived neighborhoods.

Several possible reasons were put forward by the authors. Deprived neighborhoods tend to be overcrowded and to suffer more air pollution and traffic noise, they wrote.

Physically demanding work in extreme weather is also more common among people with less money.

Green spaces, meanwhile, have been shown in earlier studies to cool their surroundings.

According to Lai, protection will have to be delivered at several levels at once. City planning was named as one of those levels.

Cooling strategies form another, as do personal decisions about where to live. Lai said such protection is needed most by the most vulnerable groups.

Extreme heat is projected to grow more frequent and more intense as populations age. That observation came from study co-author Chinmoy Sarkar of the University of Hong Kong.

Together, he said, those trends will make protecting frail people with chronic diseases a top public health priority.

A link between heat and death can be demonstrated by a study of this kind. Proof that heat caused the deaths lies beyond its reach.

Because temperatures were assigned by home address, the patients’ actual whereabouts each day remain unrecorded. Nor was any information available on air-conditioning use or on changes in medication.

Smoking and drinking habits were recorded only once, when volunteers joined UK Biobank.

Those habits may well have changed afterward. Since cases were identified through hospital admissions, milder disease that never led to admission was missed.

UK Biobank volunteers may also differ from the wider population. About 96% of the patients in this study were white. The authors wrote that the volunteers may not represent everyone in the UK with cardiovascular disease.

None of the patients was given a cooler home or a greener street during the study. How many deaths such changes might prevent therefore can’t be read from the records.

Air-conditioning use could be accounted for in future research, as could travel to places with different temperatures.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Climate.

Eagles appear to be hunting and killing adult baboons, study finds. Does that mean they could have hunted ancient human relatives?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eagles can hunt exceptionally large prey, including a baboon that weighed nearly 60 pounds (26 kilograms), a new study finds.

Some human ancestors were smaller in size than modern-day humans and weighed around the same amount as the baboons. This raises the question of whether they also might have faced eagle attacks, the researchers said.

Until now, it was thought that eagles couldn't lift nonhuman primates weighing over 29 pounds (13 kg), the researchers reported.

Scientists made the finding while conducting research in the Sahara Desert in Chad. They found the remains of at least nine adult baboons that had been killed recently by eagles. The region is home to Verreaux's eagles (Aquila verreauxii), which hunt from cliff tops, sometimes in pairs, and have talons with a grip diameter of 16 inches (40 centimeters). Grip diameter is how far the eagle’s grip extends.

The scientists found deep talon marks on the baboons' bones. These marks suggest that the eagles hunted and killed the primates and brought parts of them back to their nests, the team noted in a paper published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology.

The photo on the left shows an eagle-baboon encounter, while another image (right) features a baboon skeleton with marks of eagle predation.

The baboons were sizable, with an average estimated weight of 49 pounds (22.2 kilograms). The largest of them weighed 58 pounds (26 kg), which is similar in size to some small hominins, a group that includes humans and our close relatives that arose after the split from chimpanzees and bonobos, the researchers noted. For instance, the Australopithecus afarensis individual known as Lucy weighed about 62 pounds (28 kilograms) when she was alive in what is now Ethiopia around 3.2 million years ago.

While eagles do sometimes scavenge carcasses, this doesn't seem to be the case with the baboons. The "severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip," the team wrote in the study.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

They noted that eight out of nine of the baboons in the study were male. This suggests that the baboons were hunted, since scavenged animal remains would not favor a particular sex. Why eagles hunted mainly male baboons is not clear, and the "male sex-bias in our sample is puzzling," the researchers noted. Male primates, such as monkeys, do sometimes defend against eagles by charging at them, the team added in a statement.

There is one known example of eagles hunting and killing a hominin. The "only confirmed case is Taung Child, an infant Australopithecus who we think was taken by a large eagle around 2.8 million years ago," study first author Catherine Hobaiter, a professor at the University of St. Andrews in the U.K. who has studied primates extensively, told Live Science in an email. The Taung Child weighed around 22 pounds (10 kg).

Hobaiter noted that "several of the australopithecine species who lived around 1 [million to] 3 million years ago would be in the same weight range as the adult male baboons in our study" and would have been vulnerable to eagle attacks. Other large predators, such as hyenas and crocodiles, also would have been a threat.

Nowadays, smaller primates, such as monkeys, defend against eagle attacks by traveling together.

"Modern primate species that are predated by eagles spend time in mixed species groups — for example foraging together," Hobaiter said. "That means extra competition for the food — but the benefits of the added protection seem to be worth the cost."

Hominins may have done something similar, with different hominin species traveling together to defend against eagle attacks, she noted.

An illustration of a Verreaux's eagle hunting an adult male baboon.

Robert Simmons, a researcher at the FitzPatrick Institute of African Ornithology at the University of Cape Town who wasn't involved with the study, called the findings "fascinating." Eagles "are opportunistic — an old male or a young male baboon dispersing to another troop found on its own can become prey to an opportunistic eagle, or a pair of eagles," Simmons said in an email. In a desert region, the lack of cover can leave baboons exposed.

This is "certainly a rare occurrence," he said. But in this dry desert environment, the prey available to the Verreaux's eagles is limited, which has forced them to take on larger, more dangerous prey than is typical for a 9-pound (4 kg) eagle, Simmons explained.

W. Scott McGraw, an anthropology professor at The Ohio State University who also wasn't involved with the study, said in an email that early "hominins may have been particularly attractive targets because of their relatively small body size," especially infants and juveniles.

"Given their limited physical defenses, early hominins — and, indeed, primates more generally — likely evolved a range of behavioral adaptations to reduce their vulnerability to raptors and other predators," McGraw said. These adaptations may have included living in groups, yelling out to warn others, and selecting habitats that could offer protection from attacks.

Jesús Bautista-Rodríguez, the coordinator of the Desert Golden Eagles Project who has conducted extensive research on eagles, said that the finds were interesting but was cautious about some of the conclusions.

"I am much more cautious, however, about interpreting the remains described in this paper as evidence that the eagles actively killed healthy adult male baboons weighing over 20 kg [44 pounds]," Bautista-Rodriguez told Live Science in an email. "In my opinion, it is quite possible that some, or even all, of these individuals were already dead, dying, severely weakened or otherwise unable to defend themselves when the eagles fed on them."

He also took issue with how the baboons died, saying that more fieldwork is needed to better understand how eagles came across the baboons.

“The punctures and extensive scratches observed on the skulls and scapulae are certainly interesting and compatible with eagle talons and feeding activity," Bautista-Rodriguez said. "Nevertheless, these marks do not necessarily demonstrate that the eagle was responsible for killing the animal. They could also have been produced during the handling, dismemberment and feeding of an individual that had already died."

Hobaiter, C., Akpona, T.J.D., Kopp, G.H., Dominy, N.J. (2026). Signs of eagle predation on a 22-kg adult primate. American Journal of Biological Anthropology. https://doi.org/10.1002/ajpa.70377

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

Right now, Bose’s latest QuietComfort headphones are 45 percent off, which amounts to nearly $200 in savings. $200 for our best-tested noise-canceling headphones is an absolute steal.

The QuietComfort 2.0 makes some significant improvements on Bose’s best-selling QuietComfort noise-canceling headphones. For starters, they feature a modernized design, offering more comfortable pill-shaped earcups and a sliding, adjustable headband. They’re also slightly wider than the previous model, with cozier synthetic leather that strikes a perfect balance between a soft and secure fit.

Performance has also improved. Bose’s new proprietary TrueSpatial Technology adds another layer of immersive, natural sound alongside its best-in-class noise cancellation. It also adds improved high-fidelity lossless audio via a USB-C connection.

Senior Tech Editor Stefan Vazharov also raves about the latest QuietComforts (which, for what it’s worth, are also my go-to over-ear headphones)—we have them in our latest tech gift guide, as well.

“A sequel to a legendary product, the Bose QuietComfort (2nd Gen) headphones add welcome upgrades, headlined by spatial audio and lossless audio playback over USB-C,” Vazharov said. “I'd take them in a heartbeat for less than $200, and use the savings to grab an extra set in one more of the many available colors.”

Speaking of noise cancellation, that has gotten better with age, too. The second-generation headphones feature updated ActiveSense Tech for adaptive acoustic noise reduction, which evens out sound spikes when listening in Aware Mode. There’s also improved background noise reduction—perfect for meetings and calls.

We’re looking at a more intuitive interface, including updated button placement, easier volume control, and an easier-than-ever way to cycle through listening modes. This is as important as ever, as Bose added new modes to the equation. In addition to its usual QuietMode for full noise cancellation, there’s now Cinema Mode with layered sound for enhanced video content, Immersion Mode, and ANR off.

These are our favorite noise-cancellation headphones at full price—although at almost $400, we’d even admit that’s pretty steep. But $200 is a steal—especially for one of our top 2026 tech gift picks. Get these while you can; we don’t expect this deal to last long.
